data.title: Markets Melt Up As Stocks Snap Losing Streaks
data.description:
Wall Street roared back to life to start the holiday-shortened week, emboldened by resurgent Nvidia (NVDA) and the return of risk-on sentiment. The Dow added 1,447 points to snap a five-day losing streak. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq followed suit, the former halting a seven-day skid and the tech-heavy latter gaining 1,471 points. All three major indexes erased their Friday selloffs and logged their best single-session gain since April 2025.

NVDA popped 31.5% after CEO Jensen Huang was reinstated, though President Donald Trump's vocal role in the stunning reversal puts the AI trade on tenuous ground to some still. Nevertheless, the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) closed well below 30 today. 

Oil Moves Lower as Gold Bounces off $3,500

Oil prices deflated today as oversupply concerns weighed. January-dated West Texas Intermediate (WTI) shed 2.5% to settle at $81.35.

Gold prices gained as the AI trade and tech stocks remain on shaky ground. December-dated futures added 3.9% for the session to settle at $3,649.20 per ⁠ounce.

data.title: Tricolor Holdings Collapse: Is There A Larger Threat To The U.S. Economy?
data.description:
The failure of Tricolor Holdings raises a serious question about the American credit system. Could other lenders serving financially vulnerable borrowers be carrying similar risks, and could their failures spread into banks, private credit funds, securitized debt markets, and eventually the broader economy?

1. Credit risk. Borrowers cannot repay their loans.

2. Funding risk. Lenders lose access to the capital needed to operate.

3. Contagion risk. Losses spread to banks, investors, and other lenders, forcing them to reduce credit.

A single subprime auto lender failing is not a systemic crisis. Multiple lenders failing because they share the same funding weaknesses could become a much larger problem.

What Happened to Tricolor Holdings?

Tricolor, a Texas-based subprime auto lender and used-car dealer, filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in September 2025. The company raised more than $1.9 billion through asset-backed securities (ABS) offerings from 2020 through bankruptcy. More than $945 million in ABS principal remained outstanding at bankruptcy, according to the SEC’s August 18, 2026 enforcement announcement.

The SEC alleges former executives pledged the same auto loans to multiple creditors, manipulated delinquency data, and misrepresented the company’s financial condition. The allegations should be read in the context of the individual regulatory and criminal proceedings.

The important issue is how the company obtained financing. Tricolor originated loans, borrowed against those loans through warehouse facilities, and packaged loans into asset-backed securities sold to investors. When collateral records cannot be trusted, lenders face uncertainty over who has a valid claim on the loans and what those claims are worth.

How the Damage Reached Banks and Investors

The failure reached major financial institutions. JPMorgan Chase, Barclays (BCS) and Fifth Third Bancorp (FITB) were named in an investor lawsuit brought by holders of more than $230 million in Tricolor notes. The plaintiffs alleged the banks overlooked earlier audit warnings. The $230 million refers to the notes held by the plaintiffs. A federal judge dismissed the suit in June 2026. Reuters covered the original complaint, and Bloomberg Law reported the dismissal.

Tricolor’s financing involved major banks and institutional investors. Even when those institutions can absorb losses on one borrower, similar problems across multiple borrowers could prompt them to tighten funding for the rest of the sector.

Other Companies to Investigate

America’s Car-Mart (CRMT) — Disclosed liquidity pressure, covenant issues and substantial doubt about its ability to continue as a going concern.

Credit Acceptance (CACC) — Multistate consumer settlement announced in September 2026.

DriveTime and Byrider — Buy-here-pay-here financing models.

Exeter Finance and Westlake Financial — Nonprime auto lending and securitization.

First Brands Group — Separate corporate collapse involving complex asset-backed financing.

A shared business model is a reason to compare funding practices and credit performance. It provides no evidence of comparable misconduct.

America’s Car-Mart Is the Lender to Watch First

America’s Car-Mart’s fiscal 2026 annual filing reported $722.4 million in indebtedness and a credit-loss provision equal to 40.8% of sales. The company closed 60 dealerships during the fiscal year and ended it with 94. Its subsequent quarterly disclosures showed weaker credit performance and continued liquidity pressure. The company reported $27.5 million in unrestricted cash at July 31, down from $47 million at April 30, and disclosed covenant relief while reviewing financing and strategic options. America’s Car-Mart quarterly results.

An October report described discussions of a sale or restructuring, including a possible Chapter 11 process. It also reported that securitized loans quoted near 98 cents on the dollar. The distinction matters. A finance company can struggle to fund its operations while particular loan pools continue to perform.

Credit Acceptance Presents a Different Risk

State attorneys general announced a settlement involving $694 million in cash and debt relief over allegations concerning subprime auto lending practices. The agreement addresses consumer lending conduct. It does not establish insolvency or similar collateral fraud. Michigan attorney general’s settlement announcement.

How Widespread Is the Underlying Risk?

Federal Reserve research on buy-here-pay-here financing found that balances in that segment grew much faster than in traditional auto finance after 2018. It also found higher delinquency and active repossession rates. The same research estimated that buy-here-pay-here loans accounted for about 2% of the $1.6 trillion auto loan market in its credit-panel sample.

That small share limits the likelihood that trouble confined to buy-here-pay-here lending destabilizes the economy. The risk grows if problems with collateral verification or short-term funding appear across other lending markets.

How Nonbank Lending Connects to the Banking System

The Boston Fed’s analysis puts drawn bank lending to nonbank financial intermediaries at $1.7 trillion in early 2026. Banks had roughly another $1 trillion in undrawn commitments, bringing the total to about $2.7 trillion. At the eight largest U.S. banks, lending to these intermediaries accounted for about 20% of outstanding loans, up from 9% in 2020.

These figures describe the size of the connection. Nonbank borrowers include private equity funds and business credit intermediaries, including private credit funds. The $1.7 trillion covers this broader population and does not measure expected losses or the size of private credit alone. The Financial Stability Board separately estimated the global private credit market at $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion at the end of 2024 and flagged opaque valuations, leverage and links among financial institutions.

Are We Approaching a Systemic Financial Crisis?

More failures among weak subprime lenders — Elevated

Further losses in auto-loan securitizations — Elevated

Wider tightening of consumer credit — Meaningful

Contagion into private credit and regional banks — Plausible

Economy-wide financial crisis — Insufficient evidence

The Federal Reserve’s November financial stability assessment described the banking system as sound and resilient while identifying stress among riskier borrowers. The Bank of England has also pointed to vulnerabilities highlighted by Tricolor and First Brands. It observed that the initial failures had not led to material repricing across credit markets.

Five Signs the Problem Is Spreading

1. Additional subprime lenders issue going-concern warnings or lose warehouse financing.

2. Auto ABS downgrades spread across issuers.

3. Multiple banks increase reserves tied to nonbank finance companies.

4. Private credit funds restrict redemptions as underlying defaults rise.

5. Credit spreads widen across unrelated sectors.

The New York Fed’s third-quarter 2026 report put household debt at $19.1 trillion, with 5% of outstanding balances in some stage of delinquency. Household delinquencies measure pressure on borrowers. Bank reserves, funding terms and credit spreads can show whether that pressure is spreading to lenders and investors.

What I’m Watching Next

There are enough companies using similar financing structures to warrant serious investigation. We have evidence of multiple corporate failures, a distressed publicly traded lender, pressure on subprime borrowers and substantial links between nonbank lenders and major banks. The evidence still falls short of an imminent systemic crisis.

America’s Car-Mart, bank financing to nonbank lenders and auto securitizations are where I would look next. Can lenders verify who has a claim on the collateral? Can they withstand losses when more borrowers stop paying? The answers will help determine whether the damage stays with individual firms or spreads across credit markets.

Sources

SEC’s August 18, 2026 enforcement announcement

Reuters covered the original complaint

Bloomberg Law reported the dismissal

America’s Car-Mart quarterly results

Michigan attorney general’s settlement announcement

Boston Fed’s analysis

New York Fed’s third-quarter 2026 report

data.title: BofA Says Buy These 3 Stocks Heading Into 2027
data.description:
Bank of America analysts see several reasons to load up on Disney (DIS), Caterpillar (CAT), and Medtronic (MDT) shares as 2026 draws to a close.

DIS is entering a new fiscal year after a stronger-than-expected quarter; MDT has an investor event coming up that could clarify its earnings outlook, and CAT may earn more in the next “industrial downturn” than it did in past slumps.

The three names carry Buy ratings at BofA heading into 2027.

Why is BofA bullish on Disney stock?

Disney’s Q4 sales, operating income and earnings per share (EPS) all topped BofA analyst Jessica Reif Ehrlich’s expectations.

Adjusted EPS rose 59% to $1.77, helped by an extra week in the quarter. Disney estimates it would have earned $1.59 a share on the same adjusted basis without that benefit, still up 43% from a year earlier.

Management reiterated its forecast for double-digit adjusted EPS growth in fiscal 2027.

For investors, streaming margins offer a way to track that outlook. Disney’s subscription streaming business earned an 11.5% operating margin in fiscal 2026.

Further gains would show how much of the revenue growth Disney can turn into profit while continuing to invest in programming. DIS shares pay a dividend yield of 1.48% as well.

Why is BofA bullish on Medtronic stock?

Medtronic reports fiscal Q2 earnings on November 24, but BofA analyst Travis Steed sees a potential catalyst at the company’s Dec. 10–11 investor event.

He expects Medtronic to update its full-year outlook to exclude the diabetes business and explain how the revised numbers compare with its previous guidance.

That would give investors a cleaner starting point for estimating what Medtronic can earn as it separates MiniMed. Steed sees pre-pandemic gross margins as a longer-term goal and expects the plan to fall short of that level.

What could move MDT stock is a credible path to higher earnings per share while preserving room to invest in new devices. Note that Medtronic currently pays a dividend yield of 2.88%.

Why is BofA bullish on Caterpillar stock?

BofA’s Caterpillar thesis hinges on what the equipment maker can earn when demand cools. The bank expects profits at the bottom of the next cycle to hold above levels seen in past downturns.

Power equipment helps explain that view. Data center operators need generators, giving Caterpillar another source of orders alongside its traditional construction and mining customers.

Third-quarter sales climbed 17% to $20.7 billion, and the backlog reached a record $78.1 billion.

Caterpillar held its full-year sales growth forecast steady amid cost pressures.

Heading into 2027, the question is how quickly the company can deliver those orders and how much profit it keeps as it adds capacity.

CAT shares currently pay a dividend yield of 1.28%.

data.title: What 2022 Says About This Bounce
data.description:
Nvidia (NVDA) added $728 billion in market cap in a single session today. That’s more than the entire market cap of Costco (COST) or Netflix (NFLX).

Corey Rosenbloom said a bounce was likely before it happened. Now he’s watching one pattern from 2022 that could turn this rally into a trap.

The S&P 500 dropped about 9% last week. That slide wiped out the index’s gains for the year in just a few sessions.

Jensen Huang stepping down at Nvidia rattled the whole AI trade. Corey says the fear was legitimate.

Traders worried it marked the top of the AI cycle. Today Huang was put back in, and Nvidia ripped 32% in one session.

Corey calls Nvidia the sun of the AI solar system. When it went dark, darkness spread across the market.

When the sun came back on, everything warmed up. Dell (DELL), Micron (MU), Marvell (MRVL), Intel (INTC), Palantir (PLTR) and Qualcomm (QCOM) all rallied.

The S&P bounced about 5% today and erased more than half of last week’s loss. The Nasdaq fell 10% last week and jumped more than 7% today.

Corey flagged the VIX ahead of the break. He warned that a reading above 25 could trigger a rapid bout of selling.

The VIX spiked all the way to 40. It hadn’t run that hot since the slower selloff in March.

Corey’s Friday game plan mapped the floor too. He named 7000, a prior high, as the target if support broke.

The S&P hit that zone and bounced. Short sellers bought back their positions to lock in profits, and that buying added fuel.

Corey has a blunt warning for anyone tempted to short this tape. He says one of the worst things a trader can do is start shorting after a massive down move.

He compares it to buying hurricane insurance the day after the hurricane. Protection belongs on the books well before the storm hits.

That brings Corey to 2022. That year the S&P fell from 4800 to a support shelf near 4300.

The market staged a reflexive rally and retraced about half the drop. It stalled, rolled over and broke to new lows.

The bounces in 2023 and 2025 held. The 2022 bounce failed because inflation was a problem and the Fed was raising rates aggressively.

Rates remain high today. The Fed meets in early December.

Here’s what Corey breaks down in tonight’s video:

  • 7000 on the S&P 500 is the level Corey uses to frame his swing trades. What the market does off that level tells him whether this is a holiday rally or a 2022 repeat.

  • Corey’s Friday game plan circled 7300 as the session peak. When the market trades under the profile, he plays the move back toward the midpoint with calls or call spreads.

  • 10 of 11 sectors closed green today. Energy was the lone loser with oil down 3%, and Corey reads that as a good sign for bulls.

  • Gold rallied about 4% after traders liquidated it to cover losses and margin calls during the selloff.

Thanksgiving week tends to bring a bullish holiday drift. The week also brings more inflation data, a few earnings reports and a half day on Friday.

Corey wants to see how far this bounce runs before he trusts it. He’s tracking the next move day by day.

data.title: A Better Solution To Reform, Rather Than End, The Filibuster: Lower The Threshold To 55
data.description:
There’s no big actual economic news today (this morning’s episode of Rank: Corrupt Kleptocracy doesn’t count), so hear me out - I promise reading will only take a few minutes! - on what I think is a superior way to deal with the Senate filibuster rather than just ending it.

Let me start with the observation that the filibuster has only crippled the Senate by being coupled with the “two-track” legislative system, which allows the Senate to proceed to other business if a cloture vote fails. It is these two in tandem that have been deadly.

My thoughts all spring from this chart I saw a couple of weeks ago, detailing which party was in the majority in the Senate, and by how much, for the entire last 100 years:

To save you a lengthy exercise in parsing the  numbers, here are the important ones:

Number of years the GOP has had a 60-vote majority:  - 0 -

Number of years the Democrats have had a 60-vote majority: 18 

 - 1933-44

 - 1959-68 (including a 59-vote majority when the US only had 8 States in 1959)

 - 1975-78

 - 2009-10 (for 8 months) Note: this is the only time since Reagan was elected President in 1980 that the Democrats have had 60 votes.

But the 60-vote threshold to end the filibuster is neither sacrosanct nor of long standing. The threshold was lowered from 67 to 60 in 1975. And the “two-track” system has only been around since 1972, in response to GOP filibusters of civil rights legislation.

So, should we abolish the filibuster, since Democrats have only been able to overcome it for 8 months in the past 46 years? Certainly, that would be a “less worse” option than never being able to legislate on anything other than the budget and executive appointments. 

But it means that any time the GOP has a “trifecta” of the House, Senate, and Presidency, they would be able to enact their most extreme agenda with no power restraining them. Needless to say, this would be extremely dangerous.

And since 1980, they have had the trifecta a total of 16 years:

 - 1981-86

 - 2003-06

 - 2017-20

 - 2025-26

While each party getting to enact its agenda is better than Democrats’ for all intents and purposes never being able to enact theirs, as you can see, this is very dangerous, as about 1/3rd of the time in the past 46 years the GOP has had full control.

But let me suggest a better alternative. What happens if, instead of abolishing the filibuster, we lower the cloture limit to 55?

In the past 100 years, the GOP has had 55-59 Senate seats for only 8 years:

 - 1929-30

 - 1997-2000

 - 2005-06

But in the past 100 years, the Democrats have had 55-59 Senate seats for 20 years:

 - 1943-46

 - 1969-70

 - 1973-74

 - 1979-80

 - 1987-94

 - 2011-12

 They will have over 55 in 2027-28 as well.

If you are keeping score, the Democrats have had 55 or more seats for a total of 38 in the past 100 years, including 10 years since Reagan’s election in 1980, while the GOP has had a similar number for only 8 years in the past 100 years.

In short, lowering the majority needed to invoke cloture to 55 would greatly favor Democrats’ ability to pass their legislative agenda, while the threshold historically would prevent extreme measures by the GOP to very rare occasions.

And this could be coupled with “two-track” reform as well, if the majority were so inclined. For example, after a first failed cloture vote with a 60 threshold, a majority could vote to remove the legislation from the “two-track” regimen. After a second failed cloture vote, the threshold would be lowered to 55. And only if cloture failed would the Senate have to move on to other business.

It is not clear at all that at least 51 of the 56 Democrats in the new Senate would be willing to abolish the filibuster. But they might be willing to undertake the easier lift of simply amending it to lower the threshold for cloture to 55 votes - a better solution all the way around.

data.title: New Nvidia CEO Is The Old One: Huang Returns, NVDA Soars 35% And Bitcoin Follows
data.description:
In the end, Nvidia’s board backed down and reinstated Jensen Huang as the “new” Nvidia (NVDA) CEO. The announcement triggered a broad market rebound, sending stocks higher and adding trillions in market value. But skepticism remains high, particularly across the crypto market, where investors are still waiting for signs of a sustained recovery.

Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive on Monday, November 23, 11 days after he resigned, and the stock exploded. The new Nvidia CEO is the old one, and investors cheered. Shares jumped from about $136 to as high as $169 in pre-market trading after the 8:55 a.m. ET announcement.

That peak was 35% above Friday’s close of $125.53. The stock opened near $163 and traded around $160 shortly after, still up 27%. Crypto went along for the ride. Bitcoin (BTC.X) rose as much as 5% to about $64,100, and Ethereum (ETH-X) as much as 7%.

The reversal came a day after President Donald Trump urged the board to bring Huang back. “I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Sunday.

So how much of the scandal sell-off has Nvidia won back, and what comes next?

New Nvidia CEO: The Board Reverses Itself in Six Days

Nvidia’s board “voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang” after meetings with him, it said in its announcement. It said it was satisfied with his “candor and ability to lead.”

It is a sharp turn. On November 17, chair Harvey Jones said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and had hired a search firm for a new Nvidia CEO.

The government helped change that. The board said it heard from “senior levels of the United States government” before deciding. Based on that input, it is confident Huang’s return “poses no national security risk.” Huang resigned on November 12 after admitting an affair with a woman US intelligence suspects of spying for China.

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA,” Huang said. “I can’t wait to get back to work.”

Colette Kress, who ran the company as interim CEO, stays on as finance chief. The board’s independent investigation into the foreign intelligence effort will continue, and Nvidia said it will keep cooperating with government inquiries.

NVDA Won Back More Than Half of the Scandal Drop

To measure how much the new Nvidia CEO news repaired, we compared Monday’s price with Nvidia’s closes before and during the scandal.

Nvidia closed at $186.64 on November 6, the last session before Huang’s affair came out. By Friday it was down to $125.53, a loss of $61.11 a share. At $160, the stock has recovered 56% of that drop. At the $169 peak, it had won back 71%.

The peak took it above its close on November 12, the day Huang resigned ($166.19). Even at $160, the jump adds about $830 billion to Nvidia’s market value in a single morning.

The stock is still far from its highs. It sits 33% below its October 6 record close of $239.24, because it had already fallen 22% on AI spending worries before the scandal began.

Bitcoin’s move shows how closely crypto now trades with Nvidia. BTC jumped from about $61,100 to above $63,000 in the same minutes as NVDA, and crypto stocks such as Strategy (MSTR) also rose.

NVDA Price Analysis: $170 Is the Next Test

Nvidia stock trades around $160, below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $186, and its 200-day EMA at $202.

  • Resistance: $170, the floor from November 2025 to March 2026. Above that, $185, where the stock stalled several times last winter.

  • Support: $150, the level Nvidia broke last week, now a floor to hold.

XYZ:NVDAUSD 1D chart. Source: Hyperliquid

What comes next depends on Washington more than the boardroom. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent wants answers from Nvidia by November 25 on whether its chips reached China through shell companies. A reported SEC look at its accounting is still open. Huang is also due to testify to Congress in December.

With the new Nvidia CEO back in charge, those answers will decide whether the stock can hold above $150.

data.title: Gold Rebounds, But A Durable Recovery Remains Elusive
data.description:
Gold and global equity markets recovered on Monday after last week’s bruising sell-off. Support measures from Asian authorities helped steady sentiment, prompting short-covering. But the bounce needs to be treated with caution: the key question is whether gold can sustain its recovery in what remains a dollar-supportive environment.

Before Monday’s gains, the gold price had dropped in eight of the previous nine sessions. Even the one positive session was virtually flat. The intensity of the selling had left the metal severely oversold, making a relief rally likely, but that does not mean the market has found a floor.

Gold is already down roughly 35% from its January peak. But markets can remain under pressure for longer than expected when a powerful rally gives way to liquidation. The question is whether buyers are returning with conviction or whether short sellers are simply taking profits.


Inflation and the Fed remain obstacles

A more convincing recovery would probably require reassurance that the Federal Reserve is not about to become significantly more hawkish. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent hinted at concern over the weekend, suggesting that some believe the Fed risks making a policy mistake by overtightening.

Yet the inflation backdrop offers little comfort. Wednesday’s October core PCE release could reinforce concerns that price pressures remain persistent, keeping further monetary tightening in 2027 in the conversation. That makes it difficult to build a strong bearish case for the lofty dollar, with the dollar index at April 2025 levels. If US inflation remains sticky and rate expectations stay elevated, the dollar could remain supported, limiting gold’s upside.

Gold needs more than improved sentiment; the macroeconomic backdrop must also become less hostile.

Gold technical analysis: resistance levels to watch

Monday’s rebound can be viewed as an oversold recovery from the psychologically important $3,500 area, which gold came close to testing on Friday. The bounce may extend, but the broader technical picture remains bearish. Momentum is weak and there is little evidence of an imminent reversal.

Gold has broken below $4,000 and silver below $50, changing the psychology of the precious metals market. Dip-buying is no longer as straightforward, while short sellers have grown more confident.

The first resistance level is around $3,620, Thursday’s low, which gold broke beneath on Friday. It is now being tested from below and could act as resistance. Above that, $3,720 is another hurdle, having provided short-term support before last week’s sell-off.

More important is the broader $3,835–$4,100 resistance zone. The zone combines former bull-market support, the 21-day exponential moving average and a descending trendline.

Gold found buyers around $3,940 in June 2026 and returned to the area in late October. That recovery failed, leaving buyers exposed when selling resumed.

Unless gold can reclaim this broader resistance zone convincingly, the path of least resistance should remain lower. I would not rush to buy into the current strength; a more attractive signal would be a clear reversal pattern at lower levels or a meaningful improvement in the technical picture.

Where could gold fall if selling resumes?

The immediate downside focus is the liquidity beneath last week’s low. After a fall of almost 9% last week, stop-loss orders are likely to be clustered below the $3,500 mark, particularly among traders who tried to buy the dip.

If the rebound loses momentum and selling returns, a break beneath that psychological level could trigger another wave of selling as stops are activated. A test looks likely if the broader bearish trend remains intact.

Below $3,500, the 161.8% Fibonacci extension of the June-to-August upswing sits around $3,476. The 261.8% extension of the smaller rally that ended on 10 November is near $3,420. Beyond those levels, the next major psychological areas are $3,400 and $3,300, followed by $3,000.

For now, Monday’s recovery looks more like a relief rally within a broader bearish trend than evidence that a durable low is in place. The burden of proof remains with the buyers.

data.title: Vstock Transfer Expands Its Issuer Services Platform with Issuer-Sponsored Tokenized Shares Through a Strategic Collaboration with Metagood
data.description:
New York, United States, November 23rd, 2026, FinanceWire


Public companies and companies preparing to go public will have a single agent for shareholder records, corporate actions and tokenized ownership as the SEC’s Innovation Exemption opens U.S. markets to onchain trading

Vstock Transfer, LLC (“Vstock”), an SEC-registered transfer agent and registrar serving approximately 1,000 issuers, including companies listed on the NYSE, Nasdaq and OTC Markets, today announced a strategic collaboration with Metagood, a tokenization and lifecycle management provider for regulated digital assets, under which it plans to add issuer-sponsored tokenized shares to its suite of issuer services.

Through the collaboration, Vstock will offer public companies and companies preparing to go public the ability to issue their shares in token form, supported by the same team that manages their shareholder records, corporate actions and annual meetings. Metagood’s patent-pending platform will connect directly to Vstock’s recordkeeping system, so token holders and book-entry holders will appear on a single shareholder register, and dividends, stock splits, tender offers and shareholder votes will be processed once for every holder.

The tokens will be the company’s own shares, recorded in token form by its transfer agent. They will not be wrappers, derivatives or synthetic products. They are designed so that a token holder is a registered shareholder with the same economic and voting rights as a holder of book-entry shares. The platform is interoperable across multiple blockchains and built to add more, so an issuer’s shares can be offered on the networks its investors use.

Tokenized shares will be the latest addition to Vstock’s expanding suite of services, which spans shareholder recordkeeping, DTC eligibility and DWAC transfers, corporate actions, proxy and annual meeting services, IPO and SPAC support, and equity administration. Vstock continues to build its platform around one principle: anticipating what issuers will need next and delivering it with the responsiveness required of the capital markets.

A Governance Decision, Not Just a Technology Decision

For boards and management teams, tokenization is now a governance question as much as a technology question. Sponsoring tokenized shares through their transfer agent gives companies a way to participate on their own terms, with their official register, their shareholder relationships and their corporate actions intact.

“Companies come to us for guidance well before they come to us for a service, and tokenization is now at the top of the list,” said Yoel Goldfeder, Chief Executive Officer of Vstock Transfer. “Issuers want to know how they can offer their shares in token form, and how to do it on their own terms. This collaboration gives them a clear path. We selected Metagood because its platform was built for what a transfer agent does every day after shares are issued: paying dividends, processing corporate actions and counting every vote accurately.”

“We built our first tokenization product at Vstock years ago, and we learned that the market was not ready for it,” said Seth Farbman, Chairman and Founder of Vstock Transfer. “The rules, the exchanges and investor demand have now caught up, and small and mid-cap companies deserve access to the same tools as the largest issuers. For a growth company CEO, tokenized shares can open the door to a new generation of investors and a more direct relationship with shareholders. Whether a company is preparing for its IPO, planning an uplisting or simply evaluating its options, we want Vstock to be its first call.”

Danny Yang, Chief Executive Officer of Metagood, commented, “Our platform will let Vstock handle every dividend, vote and corporate action for token holders with the same precision it delivers for book-entry holders today.”

Companies interested in issuer-sponsored tokenized shares, or in learning more about third-party tokenization notices under the Innovation Exemption, are invited to schedule a consultation with the Vstock team at [email protected] or visit www.vstocktransfer.com.

About Vstock Transfer

Vstock Transfer, LLC is an SEC-registered stock transfer agent and registrar serving approximately 1,000 issuers, from private companies and IPOs to public companies listed on the NYSE, NYSE American, Nasdaq and OTC Markets. Founded and managed by securities attorneys, Vstock provides shareholder recordkeeping, certificate services, DTC eligibility and DWAC transfers, proxy and annual meeting services, and equity administration tools. Vstock is based in New York.

For more information, visit www.vstocktransfer.com

About Metagood

Metagood provides next generation infrastructure for regulated financial assets. Its patent-pending platform connects traditional financial systems with blockchain networks to tokenize assets and automate their lifecycle, including transfers, payments, distributions and corporate actions. Built for financial institutions, transfer agents, exchanges and issuers, Metagood enables securities, mortgages and other regulated assets to be managed more efficiently and transparently across traditional and digital markets.

For more information, visit www.metagood.com

data.title: CrowdStrike And Zscaler Building A Formidable AI Moat
data.description:
On November 23, 2026, markets received confirmation of a deal that had been rumored for days: CrowdStrike (CRWD) is acquiring Zscaler (ZS) in an all-stock deal worth nearly $43.9 billion.

Big acquisitions always raise eyebrows among investors, but CrowdStrike has an exceptional track record of integrating acquisitions, and the Zscaler deal makes a lot of strategic sense.

CrowdStrike and Zscaler together will be arguably the strongest cybersecurity company in the world, with over 10 billion in ARR (Annual Recurring Revenue) and covering all security needs with top-level AI capabilities.

The Deal

Zscaler shareholders will receive 1.135 shares of CrowdStrike common stock for each Zscaler share under this agreement. Based on current market prices, that means nearly $260.41 per Zscaler share, valuing the company at approximately $43.9 billion.

That implied price represents a roughly 34% premium to Zscaler’s Friday closing price of $194.82. Once the deal closes, existing CrowdStrike shareholders will own approximately 84.1% of the combined company, while Zscaler shareholders will own 15.9%.

Both boards unanimously approved the deal. Critically, Jay Chaudhry and his affiliates, who hold roughly 34% of Zscaler’s outstanding shares, signed binding voting agreements supporting the transaction.

Rather than walking away with a large wire transfer, Chaudhry is rolling his fortune into CrowdStrike equity, continuing to lead the Zscaler business post-close, and taking a seat on CrowdStrike’s Board of Directors.

Both companies expect the transaction to close in the second half of CrowdStrike’s fiscal year 2028 (which runs from August 2027 through January 2028), pending Zscaler shareholder sign-off and global regulatory clearances.

Financing And Valuation

Investors naturally dislike dilution, which explains why CrowdStrike stock is initially down by 8% after the announcement, as the share count will increase roughly 18% after this deal. However, the capital allocation considerations make a lot of sense on deeper review.

CrowdStrike stock was relatively expensive as the deal was being negotiated. The stock price is booming due to spectacular growth and profitability metrics, with a market capitalization near $216 billion. CrowdStrike stock is up nearly 80% year-to-date, a remarkable outperformance in a tough market for tech stocks.

Zscaler, on the other hand, had been unfairly beaten up, down more than 16% year-to-date, due to market panic over whether AI coding tools would let enterprises cheaply clone traditional SaaS products.

In terms of EV-to-revenue ratio, CrowdStrike stock is aggressively valued at almost 43 times revenue, while Zscaler trades at a much cheaper 9 times revenue.

Data by YCharts

When your currency (CrowdStrike stock) trades at a big premium and a premier strategic asset sits in the penalty box, using equity to lock in a transformational acquisition is textbook corporate finance. You are trading expensive shares for undervalued, mission-critical infrastructure.

Importantly, this acquisition is being done from a position of strength, as CrowdStrike has just reported excellent numbers for the third quarter of fiscal year 2027, which is the period ended on October 31, 2026 for the company. Both sales and earnings exceeded expectations during the quarter, and fundamental indicators keep moving in the right direction.

Total revenue reached $1.58 billion, growing 28.5% versus the same quarter in the prior year. Net new ARR reached a record $419 million, an increase of 58% and surpassing the company's guidance by more than $70 million. In a display of confidence, management raised the new ARR guidance by 790 basis points, now expecting 45% year-over-year growth for the full year.

Operating profit margin came in at 26% of revenue, with free cash flow margin above 30%. This combination of vigorous growth and strong profitability at scale is quite remarkable.

Management sees AI agents as the next major frontier in cybersecurity, as these agents are always on and can launch increasingly sophisticated attacks at unprecedented speed. Falcon Guardian, which secures and manages AI agents, is now CrowdStrike's fastest-growing product, recently surpassing $100 million in ARR in less than a year.

Revenue And Cost Synergies

Management estimates this deal could create $1 billion in annualized revenue run-rate synergies in the first 30 months and $500 million in cost savings over the next 18 to 24 months after close. Analysts are always skeptical of these projections, and for good reason, because management teams almost always overpromise and underestimate integration headaches. With this in mind, let's take a look at the numbers behind this guidance.

The press release cites 8,000 non-overlapping Zscaler customers. If we assume CrowdStrike can cross-sell Falcon to just 15% of them, that would bring 1,200 enterprise accounts at an average annual contract value (ACV) of $400,000; that alone would generate $480 million in new ARR.

CrowdStrike also has tens of thousands of customers, including massive Fortune 1000 accounts already spending millions on Falcon Flex, that do not yet use Zscaler. Converting just 600 to 800 of those large Falcon Flex accounts onto Zscaler Zero Trust SASE and AI Protect at an average ACV of $700,000 yields another $420 million to $560 million in ARR.

We can also consider deeper upsells to the more than 2,000 shared customers who now have a powerful financial and operational incentive to consolidate onto Falcon Next-Gen SIEM (streaming Zscaler logs natively at a lower ingestion cost than Splunk or Sentinel).

Based on these numbers, $1 billion in run-rate revenue synergies actually looks achievable, even slightly conservative, provided sales execution stays consistent and disciplined.

On the cost side, CrowdStrike and Zscaler will operate on a combined annual operating expense base well north of $7 billion by 2028-2029. Finding $500 million in run-rate savings represents roughly 6% to 7% of combined operating expenses, which is well within standard benchmarks for mergers in this sector.

Without touching R&D, there is a lot of room to eliminate redundant G&A in areas like audit, legal, IR, finance, and real estate overhead. The go-to-market strategy can also drive efficiencies, since both companies have large enterprise sales forces and marketing budgets targeting the same CISOs at the same conferences. I would also expect some cost savings in areas like cloud infrastructure due to scale and negotiating power after the merger.

Risk Considerations

At $43.9 billion, this is one of the largest software acquisitions in history. Given the deal's size, I think antitrust enforcers at the U.S. Department of Justice, the FTC, the European Commission, and the UK’s CMA may be paying close attention.

The bull case for approval is that CrowdStrike and Zscaler barely compete. Endpoint protection and inline Zero Trust network security are classic complementary markets.

Regulators already set a strong 2026 precedent by clearing Google’s (GOOG) (GOOGL) $32 billion Wiz deal and Palo Alto’s (PANW) $25 billion CyberArk deal. Besides, CrowdStrike can argue it needs this combination to compete effectively against even larger rivals like Palo Alto Networks, Alphabet, and Microsoft (MSFT).

We can expect intense regulatory scrutiny over bundling and tying. To ease these concerns, CrowdStrike may need to make formal interoperability commitments, such as keeping Zscaler’s open APIs working cleanly with Microsoft Defender and SentinelOne, just as Google promised Wiz would remain multicloud. This sounds doable and reasonable.

Deal limbo is another risk. Until the deal closes, CrowdStrike and Zscaler must legally operate as completely independent competitors. They cannot merge sales teams, cannot bundle Falcon Flex + Z-Flex on a single contract, and cannot share confidential pricing. In enterprise software, a 14-month limbo window is prime hunting season for rivals, and the competition will aggressively target Zscaler’s pipeline during 2027.

The good part is that the strategic partnership between CrowdStrike and Zscaler was already in place before the announcement. This means CrowdStrike and Zscaler can legally continue building and marketing their already-announced integrations through the regulatory waiting period.

George Kurtz and Jay Chaudhry are two of the most driven, intensely competitive founder-CEOs in Silicon Valley history. Both built category-defining titans from scratch, and they have strong views on architecture and go-to-market execution.

In practice, integrating a proud former standalone CEO into a subsidiary leadership role almost always creates cultural friction. Avoiding a cultural split between sales and engineering teams will require genuine executive diplomacy from both leaders, and no one can know in advance how this subtle, complex process will go.

Widening The Moat

The widening of the moat is perhaps the most important advantage in this deal. Revenue growth can be bought temporarily; economic moats, on the other hand, are what let a company compound free cash flow at high returns on capital for ten or twenty years without getting commoditized. This is essentially the most important consideration for long-term investors in CrowdStrike.

The data moat is absolutely crucial. In the AI era, foundation models are rapidly commoditizing. Open-weight models and frontier APIs are available to everyone. Proprietary, real-time, labeled operational data is the only AI moat that lasts, and CrowdStrike has just assembled a formidable data engine.

Falcon already generates trillions of security events every day from endpoints, identities, browsers, and cloud workloads worldwide. Zscaler’s Zero Trust Exchange processes more than 750 billion inline network transactions every single day across over 200 global locations.

When SafeMind correlates trillions of endpoint/identity signals with 750 billion daily inline network transactions in real time, it learns adversary patterns that single-domain competitors literally can't see. Better data trains smarter models; smarter models produce superior results. At the same time, higher efficacy attracts more enterprise customers, and more customers generate even more valuable data. That is a classic self-reinforcing AI data flywheel.

Switching costs will add another layer of competitive strength. CrowdStrike and Zscaler already had strong moats in this area before the deal, and they will only get stronger now.

Ripping out CrowdStrike Falcon across 100,000 endpoints, hundreds of cloud clusters, identity directories, and a Next-Gen SIEM packed with years of compliance logs is a multi-quarter operational nightmare and a very risky process to consider undertaking.

Replacing Zscaler’s Zero Trust Exchange, which sits directly in the live traffic path of every employee, branch office, and private application across 185+ countries, is even scarier and more complicated. It means that you are effectively rerouting the corporate nervous system while the patient is awake.

If we consider both companies together, once an enterprise runs its endpoints, identities, browser security, cloud workloads, inline Zero Trust network, and SOC automation on a single unified CRWD+ZS control plane, the switching cost becomes gigantic.

It will be incredibly hard to convince C-level management to take on millions of dollars in migration risk and the associated processes. This gigantic switching cost not only protects the business, but it also creates more opportunities for cross-selling in years to come. If you are not leaving CRWD+ZS, you will probably buy more from them in the future.

The Big Picture

Although big mergers are usually disliked for very good reasons, it is crucial to identify the exceptions to the rule. In this case, CrowdStrike is using its aggressively valued shares to buy a much cheaper business with remarkable strategic advantages. Together, the two companies are building a phenomenal data moat, perhaps the most crucial driver of success in the age of AI.

data.title: Small Business Bankruptcies Surge Due To Strain Of Inflation And Higher Interest Rates
data.description:
Pressured by inflation and elevated borrowing costs, small businesses are going bankrupt at an accelerating rate.

Small business bankruptcy filings under Subchapter V, a fast-track process for smaller firms, surged by 46 percent through the first nine months of 2026, according to Epiq AACER.

Epiq analysts identified 469,719 total bankruptcy filings through Sept. 30, an 11 percent increase from the same period in 2025. 

Epiq AACER VP Michael Hunter said he expects bankruptcy filings to continue increasing into next year. 

"The continued increase in bankruptcy filings reflects the strain of higher borrowing costs, rising household expenses, growing consumer delinquencies, and a softer job market. As cost pressures mount, more small businesses are turning to Subchapter V to reorganize.” 

American Bankruptcy Institute executive director Amy Quackenboss noted that Congress recently passed legislation that would permanently increase the eligibility limits for both Subchapter V and Chapter 13. If President Trump signs the bill into law, it will expand access to struggling businesses and families seeking relief. 

"The increase in bankruptcy filings, especially among small businesses, highlights the challenges many debtors continue to face amid persistent inflationary pressures, elevated borrowing costs, and economic uncertainty."

Larger corporations face the same economic pressure. 

According to Cornerstone Research, large corporate filings dropped slightly in the second half of 2025 and the first half of this year. The financial consulting company identified 100 large corporate filings in the 12 months ending June 30. That was down from 117 filings in the preceding 12-month period, but still 22 percent above the annual average between 2005 and 2025. 

“The continued elevated pace of large corporate bankruptcies reflects persistent challenges of the broader economic environment for companies that rely on debt financing,” Cornerstone analyst and report author Matt Osborn said.

“The data suggest that high interest rates and regulatory uncertainty, along with shifting demand and competitive dynamics within certain sectors such as manufacturing, remain the most frequently cited drivers of distress among large bankruptcy filers.” 

Cornerstone identified higher interest rates as a source of corporate strain, saying elevated borrowing costs “weighed on companies with floating-rate debt and refinancing needs.” 

Persistent inflation was also cited as a commonly cited headwind.

This Is the Federal Reserve’s Problem

These twin headwinds expose the problem the Federal Reserve faces as it tries to combat price inflation. The central bank needs to raise rates to tackle the inflation problem. However, higher rates will raise borrowing costs even higher, increasing stress on companies that rely on debt.

This is the crux of the Fed’s Catch-22. It needs to raise and lower rates simultaneously.

Corporate debt is only a fraction of the total Debt Black Hole dominating the economy. The federal government is buried under $40.5 trillion in debt, and interest expense topped $1 trillion in the last two years. Meanwhile, American consumers are burdened by well over $1 trillion in credit card debt.

Every upward nudge to interest rates increases the power of the Debt Black Hole.

So far, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh and his minions at the Fed have taken a hawkish stance. However, if history is any indication, the central bank will ultimately choose propping up the economy with more easy money over tamping down inflation.

data.title: Have Markets Hit Bottom?
data.description:
November has been an uncharacteristically bad month for financial markets. The rout has been primarily in the stock market, but the effect has been so massive that it’s influencing Forex. Across the board, stock markets have fallen, and traders have piled into safe-haven assets such as the dollar. Meanwhile, the demand for liquidity has left gold falling to levels not seen in more than a year.

However, as traders settle in on Monday, there are green shoots, with US futures broadly in the green. That’s significant because tech stocks, which are concentrated in the US, led the downside this month. After the Nasdaq fell into bear territory on an intraday basis last Friday, apparently some investors are hoping that the bottom is in, and it’s time to buy the dip. If they are right, what does that mean for Forex? Or will the trends in the currency markets continue into December?

A Short Week Could Help Revive the Market

US traders will be away from their desks for a holiday on Thursday and a shortened trading day on Friday. Typically, a notable holiday leads to lower liquidity, which increases volatility. However, in the current environment, that could provide some relief as it allows the generally more bullish retail traders to take a stronger role.

Analysts have noted that the recent drop across equities has been led by what is often called “smart money”. That is, the businesses themselves. Executives have the best insight into their sector’s performance and their own business, so when businesses sell stock or bonds, it is typically seen as a bad sign for the market. However, businesses are using the funds they are raising to fuel the massive AI build-out, which means the technical signs of distress might not align with the fundamentals. With institutional traders away for the holidays, there is likely to be less downward pressure.

How Will a Market Recovery Affect Forex?

If the bottom is in for tech stocks for now, and the market shifts into its traditional Santa Rally (December is the best-performing month of the year historically), then many recent trends in forex markets might reverse. Particularly, the strength of the dollar and the relatively weak performance of the Euro and Pound.

The Euro has come under sustained pressure over the last seven weeks as the dollar has rocketed higher amid increasing Fed hawkishness. Conversely, markets are worried about social unrest in France and what that might mean for public spending in the second-largest economy in Europe. That is the superficial read on the recent trends. However, the sell-off in US tech stocks has made them relatively undervalued, which could attract capital inflows and further support the dollar. In other words, a market rebound might not support the EURUSD.

What if There Isn’t a Rebound?

While it’s true that markets usually trend higher in December, that’s not always the case. In fact, it’s more common for a negative November to be followed by a negative December. Especially when the Fed is poised to keep raising rates.

In that scenario, the market is likely to keep piling into the dollar, which would likely come at the expense of commodity currencies like the NZD and AUD. The yen might manage to capture enough safe-haven trading to keep up with the dollar, particularly if the market still believes the BOJ will hike next month.

data.title: HPE Stock Jumps 17% As Server Price Hikes Lift Sentiment Ahead Of Results
data.description:
Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) shares surged 17% on Monday after reports that server manufacturers were raising prices to offset higher memory chip costs, boosting sentiment towards companies supplying artificial intelligence infrastructure.

The Financial Times reported on Sunday that companies selling data centre equipment, including Nvidia-powered AI servers, were significantly increasing prices to pass on rising memory costs to customers.

In some cases, the increases were as high as 45%, the report said.

The news also lifted other server manufacturers. Dell Technologies (DELL) shares gained 22%, while Super Micro Computer (SMCI) rose 14%.

HPE sells enterprise technology solutions, including servers, storage systems, networking equipment and cloud services.

The company is considered a beneficiary of the growing demand for AI infrastructure.

The stock reached an all-time high in early October but subsequently fell sharply amid a broader selloff in AI-linked shares.

Despite remaining up more than 100% this year, HPE had lost nearly half its value from its October peak as investors reassessed the outlook for AI hardware companies.

HPE earnings in focus as analysts expect record revenue growth

HPE is scheduled to report its fiscal fourth-quarter results after the market closes on Monday.

Analysts expect revenue to increase 49% year over year to $14.43 billion, representing the company's highest growth rate on record.

Adjusted earnings are forecast to more than double to $1.29 per share.

The expected growth reflects an acceleration in the company's Cloud & AI business.

Management previously guided for Cloud & AI revenue growth of 60% to 72% in the fourth quarter, compared with 25% in the third quarter.

Two factors are expected to support that performance: a record $6.8 billion backlog for AI systems and a $3.5 billion inferencing deal with a hyperscaler.

The deal was signed after the third quarter ended and involves traditional servers for the customer's internal use.

The agreement highlights demand for infrastructure used to run AI models, rather than only train them.

However, hyperscaler contracts generally carry thinner margins than enterprise business.

HPE management has indicated that operating margins are likely to moderate sequentially to a mid-teens rate.

HPE price targets and server demand remain in focus

Analysts have continued to raise their estimates despite the recent weakness in HPE shares.

Last week, UBS (UBS) lowered its price target to $52 from $66 while maintaining a Neutral rating.

The firm nevertheless identified networking and server pricing as potential sources of upside in October.

According to Koyfin, 15 of the 24 analysts covering HPE rate the stock Buy or higher, while the remaining nine have Hold ratings.

Their average price target of $70.58 represents a potential upside of 73% from Friday's closing price.

The broader market environment has weighed on AI hardware stocks in recent weeks.

Concerns include rising memory costs, discussions around data centre moratoriums, midterm election results and questions about the sustainability of AI spending.

The latest reports of server price increases could provide some support to HPE and its peers, as manufacturers seek to protect their margins from higher component costs.

However, investors will be looking to Monday's results for evidence that strong demand is translating into revenue growth while the company manages its profitability.

data.title: Finally Some Panic
data.description:
I always swear off the red-eye domestically. I hate feeling washed out the next day. However, after a successful golf tournament in CA over the weekend, I had to decide between that and a full day of travel on Monday with the markets still chaotic. So here I am. Writing in the middle of the night. Lots of charts today since so much is going on.

Thursday and Friday were ugly for the bulls. There is no other way to spin it. Friday saw some panic, but not overwhelmingly so. Almost anything and everything tech is being thrown to the wolves.

Last week, I heard a lot of “but, but, but, Paul, nothing has changed at Nvidia (NVDA). Why is the stock crashing?” Those comments started in the $170s during the rumor phase. Nothing may have changed, but the market is valuing earnings differently than it did a month ago.  One day a stock is worth 30 times earnings. Another day it’s worth 20 times. As I have said, Nvidia is a rental, not an own. Trade it until it gets repaired, assuming that happens.

The QQQ traded more than 134 million shares, the most since the tariff tantrum. That is panic. Can it get worse? Sure. Will it? I don’t know.

The Nasdaq 100, which is the index that the QQQ trades off, is below. The light and dark blue lines should act as ceilings for some time.

I decided to show a longer-term view of the Volatility Index (VIX) to include the tariff tantrum. Without it, the VIX would look like it’s in orbit, which it’s not. 30s is significant. 40s makes it tougher to invest. Could the VIX get into the 50s or 60s again? Yes. Will it? I don’t know yet. VIX moves are usually terminal. They go straight up and then die quickly. This has certainly met the criteria for a panic market bottom.

I wanted to point out two groups that have held up reasonably well during the correction: insurance and cybersecurity. Neither should lead off the bottom, but once the first snap back ends, these two are candidates to own for a while.

Consumer staples is below. It also fits the mold, but because it’s purely defensive, I didn’t want to lump it in with the other two. It’s certainly interesting and could provide some ballast.

I was going to include gold, oil, and rates, but I think I will wait until Wednesday.

Pre-market trading indicates a huge rally at the open. After the initial pullback, the bulls need to push to new highs in order to force short sellers to buy. Bears will pounce again if the gains evaporate.

Finally, you can see what we executed on Friday amidst the panic. There wasn’t any selling. 

On Friday, we bought RMQHX, QLD, and more MQQQ.

data.title: Bitcoin Bear Market Is Still Here, But Is It Nearing Its Final Stages?
data.description:
The crypto market extended its decline late last week alongside stocks, with the price structure still suggesting an ongoing five-wave bearish impulse and room for further downside. We have already seen some stabilization over the weekend, as Asian authorities stepped up efforts to stabilize regional markets. However, the current recovery is most likely just a corrective rebound before further weakness follows.

Bitcoin continues to extend lower, breaking below the July lows within the projected wave 3 of an ongoing five-wave bearish impulse. While further weakness is expected in wave 5, we could first see a temporary recovery within wave 4, which may retest the 62,000–66,000 resistance area before the downtrend resumes.

Looking at the daily chart, we are tracking a five-wave bearish impulse within wave (C) of a larger (A)(B)(C) correction. Although the bearish structure remains intact, Bitcoin could be gradually approaching the final stages of its bear market cycle, with one more decline potentially completing the larger corrective pattern.

If we take a look at BlackRock's Bitcoin ETF (IBIT), we can also identify an important potential support area for wave C of an ABC correction. Ideally, wave C could find support near the former wave 2 swing low, which coincides with the 78.6% Fibonacci retracement around the $28 level. Therefore, when looking for potential support and signs of a larger bullish reversal in BTCUSD, it is worth keeping a close eye on IBIT as well.

Meanwhile, Bitcoin's Long/Short ratio is also approaching the lower boundary of its range, suggesting that speculators are becoming increasingly bearish. Such extreme bearish sentiment could indicate that stronger support may not be far away. Nevertheless, further downside toward lower support levels remains possible as Bitcoin looks to complete its lower-degree five-wave bearish impulse, ideally by the end of 2026 or the beginning of 2027.

Big Picture:

Bitcoin remains in a bear market within a higher-degree wave IV correction. However, the one-year bearish cycle may be slowly approaching its completion, ideally toward the end of 2026 or the beginning of 2027. Once the projected wave (C) is complete, we could see more meaningful stabilization and potentially the beginning of a new bullish cycle.

Highlights:

  • Bitcoin breaks below July lows as wave 3 extends lower.

  • Temporary wave 4 recovery could revisit 62,000–66,000 resistance.

  • Another decline in wave 5 remains possible before a larger reversal.

  • Daily chart suggests wave (C) of a larger ABC correction is unfolding.

  • BlackRock's IBIT ETF highlights key Fibonacci support around $28.

  • Bitcoin's Long/Short ratio approaches the lower boundary of its range, reflecting increasingly bearish sentiment.

  • The one-year bearish cycle could approach completion in late 2026 or early 2027.

  • A larger bullish reversal may follow once the five-wave decline is complete.

data.title: The Cat That Would Not Stay Dead
data.description:
On Sunday we wrote, with apologies to our feline friends, that Monday should open with a strong dead cat bounce. We now owe the cat a further apology. Nvidia's (NVDA) board announced this morning that Jensen Huang has been reinstated as president and chief executive, effective immediately. The stock is up some 34 percent from Friday’s close, hoisting the entire market behind it, led, as it nearly always is now, by AI-dominated technology. By 9:53 a.m. Central time the S&P 500 was up 5 percent. This is not a bounce. The cat has been revived to live another life.

We are not surprised that Mr. Huang is chief executive again; criminality was always unlikely. The timing is the shock. Only eleven days ago the board accepted his resignation, offered, we assume, under the threat of dismissal, and the Associated Press reports that the board had rebuffed his offer to return only days before today’s reversal. Federal and state inquiries remain open, “Yet after a brief round of meetings the directors voted unanimously to restore him, citing input from senior levels of the United States government” and their confidence that his return “poses no national security risk.”  Attorney General Todd Blanche had confirmed that the government has no evidence of unlawful conduct by Jensen Huang.

In our view, Mr. Huang grossly violated the company’s code of conduct. But a founder of his consequence to the company, and to the global economy, is a man for whom rules are apparently written in pencil. The board set its ethical concerns aside and accepted the government’s quick opinion that don’t see any criminal exposure for knowingly selling restricted chips to a Chinese shell company. Moralists may object. Markets, which are not moralists, have voted with tremendous relief.

We were looking for an inflection rebound this week, led by technology. We got a resurrection instead. This rocket-ship rally in tech this morning will stall, as such ascents do. But our 6,800 to 7,000 target zone for an S&P 500 low should now hold through the ensuing retracements, in December and again in January. CNN’s Fear and Greed Index closed Friday at an extreme reading of 10 as the S&P 500 reached ideal support, which adds to our confidence that the rally will find good footing once the near-term euphoria wears off.

Our portfolio is chasing technology and financial stocks higher this morning and will use dips to put more of our excess cash to work. Today’s news accelerates our expectation of a fourth-quarter bottom, a period during which investors can add incrementally rather than heroically.

The road ahead still has political obstacles. The first half of 2027 carries a political overhang: the prospect of fees, regulation and permitting obstacles for the AI buildout. But the AI bull market will continue.

A cat, the proverb holds, has nine lives. Nvidia has spent one of them in eleven days. Investors would be wise not to assume the supply is inexhaustible.

data.title: Six Degrees Of Gold Price Distortion
data.description:
Gold fell about 9% last week, its worst drop since March. Associated selling mostly came from leveraged funds in the futures market, not from physical gold holders. Here’s why that matters.

Gold closed Friday near $3,514 an ounce. Silver fell even harder, shedding about 16% to close the week near $41.

There were a number of headline reasons attached, including ‘the strong dollar’. But the U.S. dollar only rose by about 2% over the same period, so that logic is shaky at best, as are the other explanations being thrown around, including Federal Reserve rate hikes, rising yields and inflation fears.

The Consensus Does Not Add Up

One of the most prevalent cited triggers is that December Fed hike odds have jumped to about 96%. Another is that near-5% risk-free money stemming from Treasury yields raises the cost of holding a so-called zero-coupon asset, a favored (and boring) headline that ignores the long-term, wealth-preserving value of gold. The other highlighted fear alleged to be spooking investors (again, on paper) is inflation.

Yet the 10-year yield more than doubled from under 2% in 2022 to above 4% by 2024, and gold didn’t fall through the Fed’s hiking cycle; it climbed. From early 2024 through January’s record, with the yield holding between 4% and 5%, gold nearly tripled. The one-point rise to near 5% in recent months does not offset a 37% drop from January’s intraday record near $5,589.

Inflation is cooling too, with October consumer prices up 0.4% after 0.6% in September. None of these changed much last week in a way that would cause such a violent drop in gold.

Last week’s acute paper-selling unfolded in three phases, with the final one wreaking the most havoc.

What unfolded last week, across Monday and Tuesday’s trading, was mostly flat and orderly, with gold prices trading in a range around $3,860. Then, last Wednesday and Thursday, gold drifted lower following the release of the October FOMC minutes, down about 5% over those two days.

However, leading into Friday, the price dropped sharply amid forced liquidation and margin calls. That last leg took gold to a 9% loss on the week and silver’s loss to about 16%, in a matter of hours.

Now, if you’re keeping score, what we’ve seen is that repeated macro headlines and self-reinforcing selling pressed gold down by 5% over two days. But acute forced selling took almost that much off gold again in a few hours on Friday, and roughly twice as much off silver prices.

Looking at the 3 charts featured below, you can see what happened and when.

This is pivotal because 6 technical forces have driven paper gold prices lower.

1. Leveraged Funds Sold 53 Tonnes of Gold Futures

Leveraged funds have been cutting gold futures for weeks. COMEX managed-money net longs fell about 53 tonnes in October. That is roughly $7 billion, by the World Gold Council’s estimate. The selling carried into last week. Gold broke $3,800, then $3,700, then $3,600. Trend-following models automatically sell what is falling without asking why or contemplating fundamental value or supply and demand. These are leveraged futures positions sold into a falling price.

2. CME Percentage Margins Forced More Selling

Since January 2026, the CME (Chicago Mercantile Exchange), where gold and silver futures trade, sets gold and silver margins as a percentage of notional value, and not of a fixed amount. So, when volatility spikes, as it did last week, the CME can raise that percentage, increasing the collateral a leveraged trader must post. Traders who can’t or won’t post more will sell paper products instead. The move aggravates selling into an already falling market and pushes prices down even faster.

3. The Rising Dollar Dragged Gold Down Mathematically

The dollar index climbed toward 104 last week, a 19-month high. Because gold is priced in dollars worldwide, when the dollar gains relative to other currencies, gold effectively costs more in euros, yen and yuan, which can put downward pressure on its dollar price. Systematic funds, the computer-driven traders that buy and sell automatically on price signals rather than on fundamentals, sell the whole commodity complex when the dollar rises, disregarding each metal’s own supply and demand. Copper fell to a four-month low, its weakest since July, and oil fell with gold.

4. Funds Had to Sell Gold to Cover Other Losses

Much of last week’s paper gold selling was a casualty of the broader tech selloff. Nvidia reported a 103% jump in revenue on November 17, but a broad AI selloff dragged its shares down anyway, amid fears of tighter AI regulation under the new Democrat-controlled Congress and doubts about AI spending. Then Anthropic went public on November 19 in the largest IPO ever, and its shares fell about 9% the next day. By November 20, the Nasdaq had purged its entire 2026 gain and the S&P and Dow had fallen into correction territory. Leveraged funds facing losses across their portfolios can be forced to raise cash, including by selling profitable positions. Gold, which had delivered substantial gains before the recent decline, was an obvious potential source of liquidity.

5. Futures Fell While Central Banks Bought 321 Tonnes

The largest gold ETF, SPDR® Gold Shares GLD, recorded about $1.4 billion in outflows over the past 30 days, reflecting selling pressure through the ETF market. Central banks bought 321 tonnes of physical gold in the third quarter, up 42% year on year, with the People’s Bank of China adding 63 tonnes and Poland 40. That buying came before the selloff, so it sets the backdrop rather than offsetting Friday’s selling. COMEX bullion holdings actually rose through November’s price decline, and in the midst of last week’s selloff, I spoke with a number of physical gold brokers, who reported gold bar and coin buying and no selling.

6. Speculative Longs Already Cut 8% Before Larger Drop

Hedge funds were already cutting their long gold exposure before last week’s sharpest selling. According to the CFTC Commitments of Traders report, managed-money net longs, which are the bets that hedge funds place on higher gold prices, fell about 8% in the week ending November 17, to 102,942 contracts. (That report only captures positions through Tuesday.) Once gold broke $3,800 and then $3,700 between Wednesday and Friday, momentum selling accelerated. The full extent of that later liquidation won’t be visible until the next CFTC report.

What this Gold Price Distortion Means

As ugly as it was, this forced selling is not the biggest danger in these sorts of programmed selloffs. The danger is investors who experience the violent drop let emotions take over while deciding that everything is broken and move to sell healthy, well-funded companies out of fear.

Exchange-traded funds amplify it mechanically, because selling a gold-miner ETF like the VanEck Gold Miners ETF GDX, or the junior-miner VanEck Junior Gold Miners ETF GDXJ, forces the fund to sell a slice of every stock it holds, dragging strong miners and weak ones down together regardless of each company’s own value.

That panic is exactly what institutional investors and more patient money thrive on and wait for. Wall Street waits for panicked sellers to take prices down, and for programmed trading to do much of that work automatically, so they can swoop in. Central banks and physical buyers buy the discount in the meantime.

Because this move is technical, and not based on fundamental factors like supply and true demand, any slight shift in the narrative, whether a softer dollar or a Fed signaling it may hold rates while assessing incoming data, could help reverse the momentum selling and trigger short covering. That can send paper gold back up as fast as it fell.

Now, I can’t say when that tide will definitely turn, or that there won’t be more chop along the way, but I can say that the Fed’s next announcement, on December 9, 2026, will be a pivotal point.

data.title: Why Funded Traders Often Lose The Account Right After The First Payout
data.description:
A first payout from a funded account feels like proof. The rules were followed, the target was met, and real money left the account. Yet a surprising number of those same accounts are gone a few weeks later.

The pattern has a plain explanation. After a payout, many traders raise their size or relax a rule they kept while working toward it. The trailing drawdown limit does not change. A modest increase in risk per trade against a fixed limit moves the odds of losing the account much more than it moves expected income, and a short simulation shows by how much.

What changes after the payout

Three things tend to shift at once. Confidence rises, because the payout looks like evidence of skill, even though it usually rests on a few dozen trades. Income goals rise, because the trader now knows what a payout feels like and wants the next one to be larger. Caution falls, because the money already withdrawn feels safe and the remaining balance starts to feel like house money.

None of this changes the arithmetic of the account. The trailing limit still sits the same dollar distance below the highest balance. In many programs, the room is even smaller after a withdrawal, because the payout comes out of the balance while the floor stays where it was. The trader feels richer at the moment the account has the least spare room.

The simulation

To keep the numbers generic, I modeled a trader with a 48% win rate, winners of 1.5R and losers of 1R, a positive edge of 0.2R per trade. The account has a $2,000 trailing limit that follows the highest balance, and the trader starts the post-payout period with the full $2,000 of room. Each risk level was run on 50,000 simulated accounts over the next 100 trades.

Before the payout, the trader risked $100 per trade, which is room for 20 full losses. I compared that with $150 per trade, which is 50% more, and $200 per trade, which is double.

Caption: Generic simulation of 50,000 accounts with a 48% win rate, winners of 1.5R and a $2,000 trailing limit. Left: one sequence of trades played at $100 and at $200 risk; the larger size reaches the trailing floor. Right: share of accounts that hit the limit within 100 trades at each risk level.

The left panel shows one sequence of trades played at both sizes. After 35 trades, the doubled account is $2,500 ahead. The next 20 trades bring 16 losses and 4 wins, starting with eight losses in a row. At $100 risk, that stretch costs $1,000, and the account keeps trading. At $200 it costs $2,000, the full limit, and the account closes at trade 55. Runs like this are ordinary for this trader: about one in five of the simulated 100-trade sequences contains at least eight losses in a row.

The right panel shows the same effect across all 50,000 accounts. At $100 risk, about 1% of accounts hit the limit within 100 trades. At $150, the figure is 10%. At $200 it is 30%.

Expected income moves much less. Counting a lost account as zero and a surviving account as its profit, the average result rises from about $2,000 at $100 risk to about $2,900 at $150 and about $3,400 at $200. A 50% size increase adds 46% to expected income and makes losing the account about nine times as likely. Doubling size adds 68% to expected income and makes losing the account about 28 times as likely.

Why the trade-off is so lopsided

The limit is fixed in dollars, while every loss scales with size. At $100 risk, the account can absorb 20 full losses from its high. At $200, it can absorb 10. Losing streaks are just as long after a payout as before it, so the same stretch of trades now consumes twice as much of the room.

Income grows at most in proportion to size, and only on the accounts that survive. The chance of a drawdown deep enough to reach the limit grows much faster, because a trailing limit needs only one bad stretch to close the account.

What this means for funded accounts

For a funded trader, losing the account costs more than the drawdown itself. It ends the stream of future payouts and usually means paying for and passing a new evaluation before trading again. For a trader whose goal is steady withdrawals, a higher average payout bought with a much higher chance of losing the account is a poor exchange.

A sizing procedure for after the payout

1. Write down your pre-payout risk as a count of losses: the distance to the floor divided by risk per trade. In the example, $2,000 of room at $100 risk is 20 losses.
2. After the payout, measure the room again from the actual balance and floor. If the withdrawal reduced it, reduce risk per trade so the count stays the same.
3. Raise size only when the room itself grows, for example after the floor stops trailing.
4. Keep the rules that produced the payout, including any daily loss stop, for at least as many trades as it took to earn it.
5. If you do raise size, do it in small steps and recompute the loss count each time. A position size calculator (https://puravidaedge.com/position-size-calculator) converts the room and the risk per trade into contracts or lots.

Limitations

The model uses fixed outcomes of +1.5R and -1R and treats trades as independent. Real results vary in size, and losses tend to cluster in difficult conditions, which would make every probability above higher. Trailing rules also differ: some limits trail only at the end of the day, some stop trailing once the balance reaches a set level, and some programs add daily loss limits. The simulation also assumes the edge stays the same after the payout, while relaxed rules often weaken it, which would push the risk higher again.

Takeaway

A payout does not give the account more room to absorb losses. Before raising size, measure the room in units of risk and keep that count where it was when the payout was earned. In this model, the trader who kept size unchanged gave up some expected income and kept the account in about 99 of every 100 cases.

This article is educational and is not financial advice. All figures come from a generic simulation and describe that simulated trader only. They are not results of any real account, strategy, or product.

The author is the founder of Puravida Edge, which builds systematic, rules-based trading strategies and risk tools for futures and forex traders.
