data.title: The “Trump Put” Gets Exercised Again.
data.description:
Today was a “rip-up-the script” day.  A headline that says “Nasdaq 100 Pares Gains to 7%” is prima facie evidence of that.  My original intention today was to unpack Friday’s meltdown and to discuss questions about whether we might be nearing the unknown strike price of the “Fed Put.”  Instead, we discovered that the “Trump Put” was struck at roughly 90% moneyness when the administration acknowledged that it was behind Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as CEO of Nvidia (NVDA).  It was clearly done to arrest the market selloff.

By my reckoning, this was the third time that the “Trump Put” was exercised during the second Trump administration.  The first was in April 2025, in the aftermath of the “Liberation Day” tariffs, when the administration reversed course on the most egregious examples.  (We speculated in March 2025 that it may have been tested then as markets got nervous about potential tariffs.)  It was then exercised in March 2026, after the start of hostilities in the Persian Gulf, when a stream of hopeful Truth Social posts about peace talks emerged.  Several followed as the market morphed from a news-driven selloff into a huge AI-spurred rally. 

Today, the President confirmed what we all suspected when the NVDA news broke this morning when he said “I’ve been speaking to the board directly and indirectly, and I felt very strongly about it.”  Yesterday, on CBS’ Face the Nation, Treasury Secretary Bessent hinted that a softer stance toward Huang might be in place, something that fit with the President’s public comments favoring Huang’s reinstatement.  And amazingly, the President all but admitted it to a PBS White House reporter who tweeted this about 30 minutes before the NVDA news broke today:

Source: X, @ElizLanders

Today is certainly the mother of all relief rallies, and deservedly so.  With one fell swoop we eliminated specific concerns about leadership at ackone of the flagship technology companies, and potentially eased concerns about “the central bank of AI” needing to tighten its monetary policies.  It also abruptly reversed a cascade of selling that climaxed on Friday afternoon.  As we left for the weekend, stocks had failed to hold the 7,000 level on the S&P 500 (SPX) and closed near their lows.  That level had been providing modest support before another piece of negative news about NVDA hit the wires.  A final spurt of pre-weekend jitters, stop-loss orders, and possibly some forced selling by leveraged investors contributed to the malaise.

As a result, I was asked whether the recent selloff might trigger the “Fed Put.”  Quite frankly, I was highly dismissive of that notion.  As we have discussed previously, the Federal Reserve has taken measures to stabilize markets, but only when credit markets are impaired.  That is a key part of their role, the third leg of the “dual mandate,” so to speak.  Credit market concerns adversely affect stock prices, so when the Fed intervenes to assuage those issues, stocks typically benefit.  That was the case when the “Fed Put” was born during the Crash of 1987.  But when stocks fall without impacting credit markets, as was the case last week, the Fed remains on the sidelines.  That might have brought dissents about a hike at the upcoming FOMC meeting, but those appear to be unlikely once again today.

So, what comes next?  NVDA and much of the tech industry will do their best to go about their business, which is rightfully welcomed by the market.  A wide range of stocks and markets have clawed back a significant portion of last week’s losses, improving the technical backdrop, hopefully along with traders’ balances.  Many will want to enjoy the relative respite of a short week (we are closed Thursday for Thanksgiving and have a half-day on “Black Friday”).  Going forward, the incoming Congress will likely have copious questions about the events surrounding Jensen Huang’s alleged entanglement with a Chinese spy and what the Commerce and State Departments knew about it, but those won’t begin in earnest until after New Year’s.  Until then, the health of the market will likely be most affected by investors’ perceptions about whether we can resume business as usual amid a backdrop of higher rates and concerns that have not been fully put to rest by today’s events.

data.title: Walmart Produces Better Than Expected Revenue But Lower FCF - Does WMT Have Much Upside?

Walmart Inc. (WMT) reported strong Q3 revenue at the pre-market open on Nov. 19, beating forecasts. However, free cash flow (FCF) fell 31% YoY, and FCF margins were lower. Nevertheless, management raised its 2027 guidance and analysts raised their price targets. But if WMT is near a peak, what's the best play?

WMT closed at $127.95 on Friday, Nov. 20, up 1.52% and was higher than the Nov. 18 close of $127.36. Moreover, since hitting 6-month lows of $103.92 on Sept. 30 and $103.09 on Aug. 28, WMT is up 24%. 

WMT stock - Barchart - Nov. 20, 2026 

But can it really rise another 24% from here in the next 6 months? Probably not.

For one, analysts' price targets are only slightly higher than before (see my last Barchart article on Nov. 9, “Unusual Put Options Volume in Walmart Ahead of Earnings Next Week - Is WMT Set to Drop?”).

For example, Yahoo! Finance's survey of 43 analysts showed an average $127.97 price target (PT) before earnings. Now it's $135.90. The same with Barchart: $129.13 before and $137.90 now.

That's only about $10 higher, or 7.0% upside. Not much to write home about.

Let's look at this more carefully and how to play WMT now.

Tepid FCF But Higher Guidance

Walmart's Q3 revenue rose 5.2% YoY to $188.8 billion and 6.1% for the 9 months to Oct. 31, 2026. That was $1.58 billion, or about 0.82% higher than the $187.3 billion forecasted by analysts, according to Seeking Alpha.

Marginal revenue increases count a lot for free cash flow, given its small margins. Nevertheless, FCF fell over 31.6% from $1.882 billion in last year's Q3 to $1.286 billion this Q3, based on Stock Analysis data.

That means its FCF margin (i.e., FCF as a percent of revenue) fell from 1.05% last year to just 0.68% this Q3. More importantly, over the last 12 months (LTM), its FCF margin dropped from 2.17% to 1.73% (i.e., $12.9 billion LTM FCF vs. $ 15.26 billion last year).

However, management raised its revenue guidance. That seemed to cheer analysts and potentially raise their FCF forecasts. The company said it expects revenue this year (ending Jan. 31, 2027) to grow by 4.9% to 5.2%. That's up from the 4.0% to 5.0% growth it expected in Q2. 

This is based on $706.4 billion projected by management for FY 2026 (ending Jan. 31, 2026). In other words, they expect sales to range between $741 billion and $743.1 billion.

Forecasting FCF 

The problem with this is that analysts already have much higher FY 2027 revenue forecasts: +6.7% to $753.77 billion, according to Yahoo! Finance. So, this may mean analysts are wrong by being too optimistic, or Walmart is purposely underestimating its current-year sales.

Therefore, if sales come in lower than expected (i.e., lower than a 6.7% growth rate, depending on how well Q4 works out, the stock could falter.

Moreover, next year's sales forecasts are even higher. For example, the average analyst forecast is for $785.41 billion, another 4.2% gain. So, lower Q4 performance could reduce those FY 2028 forecasts.

In addition, assuming the company makes a 1.85% FCF margin, as it has average on an LTM basis for the last 4 quarter (see Stock Analysis data), FCF will be just $14.53 billion:

  $785.41b FY 28 revenue x 0.0185 = $14.53 billion FCF

That is 12.9% higher than its Q3 LTM figure of $12.9 billion, but still lower than $14.923 billion in FCF in 2025 (FY 2026).

Nevertheless, let's assume that the 12.9% gain in FCF leads to a higher price target (PT).

Valuing WMT Stock

For example, using a 1.50% FCF yield (i.e., 66.67x FCF), Walmart's stock could be worth $968.7 billion (i.e., $14.53b/0.015). That's still 4.56% lower than its present market cap of $1.015 trillion.

In other words, the PT should be 4.56% lower than $127.95, or $122.06 per share.

Only if we use a 70-times multiple is WMT stock even worth its present price (i.e., $14.53b x 70 = $1,107 billion).

The point is that WMT stock looks close to fair value. There is no margin of safety here.

Shorting OTM Puts and Put Credit Spreads

This could mean it might make sense to wait to buy WMT stock. However, one short-term play is to set a lower potential buy-in point by shorting near-term out-of-the-money (OTM) puts.

For example, the $115.00 strike price put contract expiring Dec. 24 has a $0.72 midpoint premium. That strike price is 10% lower and gives the investor a potential buy-in point of $114.28, or 10.68% below Friday's close.

WMT puts expiring Dec. 24 - Barchart - As of Nov. 20, 2026

Moreover, the investor collects $72 after posting the $11,500 in collateral. That works out to a monthly yield of 0.626%, or about 7.51% annually (assuming it can be repeated monthly).

There is a good chance of success here, since the delta ratio is only -0.116, implying an 88.4% chance that WMT won't drop to $115.00 by Dec. 24.

Nevertheless, for investors willing to take on more risk, buying the $110 put as well provides a higher one-month expected return (ER).

The spread income is $72-$34, or $38, with only $500 required as collateral (i.e., ($115-$110) x 100). That means the at-risk capital is just $462, and the ER is 8.22%

  $38/$462 = 0.08225 = 8.225% ER

However, the investor could lose all the collateral if WMT drops to $110 by Dec. 24.

The bottom line is that WMT may be near a peak. One way to play it is to short OTM puts and/or invest in a WMT put credit spread.

data.title: Ten Losses In A Row Is A Position-Size Question, Not A Strategy Question
data.description:
Most traders judge a method by its win rate and its average winner. Fewer ask the question that decides whether they will still be trading next year: what does a bad run do to the account at the size I trade?

A losing streak is not a sign that a method is broken. It is a statistical certainty for almost any method that trades often enough. The part you control is the damage, and that is settled by one number you choose before the first trade: the share of the account you risk on each position.

The position: Pick your risk per trade by asking what a 10-trade losing streak would do to the account, not by asking how much you could make on the next winner.

Streaks are more common than they feel

Assume each trade is independent of the last, which is generous to the trader, since real losses tend to cluster when market conditions shift. Even then, long streaks turn up routinely.

These are the chances of seeing at least one losing streak of a given length somewhere in 200 trades. I calculated them myself, assuming each trade is independent:

  • Win rate 50%: a streak of 6 or more losses, about 80%. A streak of 8 or more, about 32%. A streak of 10 or more, about 9%.

  • Win rate 40%: a streak of 6 or more, about 99%. A streak of 8 or more, about 75%. A streak of 10 or more, about 38%.

Plenty of profitable trend-following and breakout methods win less than half the time and make their money on the size of the winners. For a trader like that, eight losses in a row over a year of active trading is roughly a three-in-four event. It should be planned for, not treated as bad luck.

What the same streak costs at different sizes

Here's the arithmetic on a hypothetical $25,000 account. Each loss is a fixed percentage of the current balance, so the dollar risk shrinks a little as the account falls. The "drawdown" is the fall from the starting balance.

Risk 1% per trade

  • 5 losses: about $23,775 left, a 4.9% drawdown

  • 10 losses: about $22,610 left, a 9.6% drawdown

  • 15 losses: about $21,501 left, a 14.0% drawdown

Risk 2% per trade

  • 5 losses: about $22,598 left, a 9.6% drawdown

  • 10 losses: about $20,427 left, an 18.3% drawdown

  • 15 losses: about $18,464 left, a 26.1% drawdown

Risk 5% per trade

  • 5 losses: about $19,345 left, a 22.6% drawdown

  • 10 losses: about $14,968 left, a 40.1% drawdown

  • 15 losses: about $11,582 left, a 53.7% drawdown

Risk 10% per trade

  • 5 losses: about $14,762 left, a 41.0% drawdown

  • 10 losses: about $8,717 left, a 65.1% drawdown

  • 15 losses: about $5,147 left, a 79.4% drawdown

The formula behind every row is the same: balance after n losses = starting balance × (1 − risk per trade)^n.

The method is identical in every row: same entries, same exits, same win rate. Only the size changes. At 1% a ten-loss streak is an irritating month. At 5% it takes away 40% of the account. At 10% it is close to the end of the account.

Why the hole gets deeper than the drawdown suggests

The table understates the problem, because getting back is harder than falling. A gain is measured on the smaller balance that is left, so the percentage needed to recover is always larger than the percentage lost. The general rule is gain needed = loss ÷ (1 − loss).

Apply it to the ten-loss rows above:

  • 1% risk: a 9.6% drawdown needs about a 10.6% gain to get back to $25,000.

  • 2% risk: an 18.3% drawdown needs about 22.4%.

  • 5% risk: a 40.1% drawdown needs about 67%.

  • 10% risk: a 65.1% drawdown needs about 187%.

The Margin Report sets out this lopsided recovery arithmetic in its column on why a 50% loss needs a 100% gain, with a worked example and a case for writing a drawdown limit into a plan before trading starts. The point here is narrower. The size you pick decides which row of that recovery table a normal losing streak drops you onto.

Three rules that follow from the numbers

1. Size from the streak, not from the setup. Before choosing a risk per trade, decide the largest drawdown you could sit through without abandoning the method, then check what a 10-loss run costs at your size. If 10 losses at 3% (about a 26% drawdown) is more than you could stomach, 3% is too big, however good the next chart looks.

2. Cut size on the way down, by rule. Many traders write a step-down into their plan, for example halving risk per trade after a set drawdown and stopping to review after a deeper one. Cutting size slows the fall exactly when your judgment is under the most pressure. Set the levels in advance. Deciding them mid-streak tends to produce either paralysis or revenge trading.

3. Count open risk, not just per-trade risk. Five open positions at 2% each, all in the same sector, can behave like one 10% position on a bad day. A per-trade limit only means something if correlated positions are counted together.

Where this does not apply

The table assumes a loss is roughly the amount you planned to risk. A stop is not a guarantee. A stock can gap through it on news or earnings, and a trading halt can freeze an exit, so real losses can be larger than planned, especially in small caps and around scheduled events. That argues for smaller sizes, not larger ones.

It also assumes you are trading the same method throughout. If a streak runs well past anything your testing or records suggested, the problem may be the method or the market regime, not luck, and no sizing rule fixes a method that has stopped working.

Finally, for long-term investors adding new money every month, a drawdown in the balance can be hidden by deposits. Track the portfolio's own return separately from contributions so the real loss stays visible.

The takeaway

You can't choose whether a losing streak arrives. You can choose what it costs. Run the 10-loss test on your current risk per trade before the market runs it for you.

data.title: Nvidia Reclaims Its Trend-Line: Bottom Or Bounce?
data.description:
Nvidia (NVDA) reclaimed its rising trend-line today after a decisive break below it on Friday. And it did it in historic fashion, with the stock on pace for the biggest one-day gain in market value ever recorded. Even so, I’d be cautious about putting too much faith in a one-day bounce. Technically, there’s still a lot of damage to repair.

The counter argument to this though is just how many times we’ve seen V-shaped bottoms in this market, where panic selling kicks in and a rally follows almost instantly. So Nvidia is at a crossroads, and from here, both scenarios are quite plausible.

What happened to Nvidia stock?

On Friday, Nvidia dropped 14% after a report that the SEC is looking into its accounting. It closed at its lowest level of the past year, well below the rising trend-line that has supported the stock for years, and capped off its worst week since 2008.

Then this morning, Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, less than two weeks after accepting his resignation. The stock exploded higher by roughly 30%, adding over $1 trillion in market value in a single session. That’s nearly double the old record.

Why I’m cautious about a one-day bounce

A huge green candle feels great, but it doesn’t erase what happened over the last six weeks. Even after today’s rally, Nvidia is still more than 30% below its October record.

The chart also shows how much work is left. NVDA is pushing into resistance right now at the $165 level. That level was the breakout point last August and held as support this spring. Today, it’s pushing back.

Above that is the old trend-line near $175. Two weeks ago, I wrote that this same line, then sitting around $171, was the line in the sand for Nvidia. It broke, and the stock fell another 25% after that. Now it’s overhead resistance.

Beyond that, the 50-day and 200-day moving averages are both up around $205. The 50-day is rolling over hard and getting close to crossing below the 200-day.

And the SEC report hasn’t gone anywhere (though rumors it might be dropped). Huang’s return answers one question, but not that one.

Is this a V-shaped bottom for Nvidia?

Here’s the case for the bulls, and it’s a good one. Some of the most powerful rallies start exactly like this. The selling gets so extreme that everyone who wanted out is out, and then one piece of news flips the whole thing around.

Friday had a lot of the signs of capitulation: a 14% drop, the worst week since 2008, and every major chip stock in the red. Today, it reversed all at once.

There’s even history on this exact chart. The last time Nvidia tested this rising trend-line was the April 2025 selloff, and that turned into a V-shaped bottom that sent the stock to new highs. Most people didn’t believe that bounce either.

How I’d trade Nvidia from here

I’m not chasing a stock that’s up 30% in a day straight into resistance. That’s a recipe for buying the high.

For the bulls, I want to see two things. First, a close above $165, and then the $175 trend-line. Second, if the stock pulls back, I want it to hold above the rising trend-line it just reclaimed, around $145. A higher low there would go a long way toward confirming a real bottom.

For the bears, a failure back below that trend-line would be worse than the first break, because it means the reclaim didn’t stick. Friday’s lows would come right back into play.

Either way, I know exactly where I’m wrong before I put on the trade. Plan your trade, manage your risk, and the profits will take care of themselves.

data.title: Honda’s Radical Fix For EVs’ Biggest Flaw
data.description:
I love my Tesla (TSLA) Model Y.

And apparently a lot of my readers do too. Like Bruce C. who messaged me: “I own a 2026 Tesla Model Y. I LOVE IT! Every owner that I’ve talked to absolutely LOVES their Tesla.”

There’s just one thing I wish I could change about owning an electric vehicle (EV).

Charging.

If you’re driving around town and can plug in at home every night, charging isn’t usually much of an issue.

But what happens when you want to take a long road trip?

You have to think about how far your battery will take you, where you’ll stop to recharge and how long you’ll have to wait before getting back on the road.

And if you’re driving an electric truck carrying thousands of pounds of cargo across the country, those problems compound exponentially.

I always thought it would be amazing if you could charge your electric vehicle without ever having to stop driving.

And today, Honda (HMC) is developing a technology that could make this dream possible.

The Road Charger

Last month, Honda announced it’s developing a technology that could fundamentally change how electric vehicles get their power.

And it’s based on something we use every day.

The roads we drive on.

Working with Japanese construction companies Taisei (TISCY) and Taisei Rotec, Honda has developed a system that can wirelessly transfer electricity from equipment buried beneath the pavement to vehicles driving overhead.

The technology uses electromagnetic induction, the same basic principle behind the wireless charging pads you can use for your smartphone.

Coils embedded in the pavement create a magnetic field that transfers electricity to a receiver mounted underneath a vehicle.

And the vehicle doesn’t have to stop for any of this to happen. It can keep driving while its battery receives electricity.

Honda plans to begin testing the technology on a public highway during Japan’s fiscal year 2027. The company wants to demonstrate that it can deliver up to 150 kilowatts of power to moving vehicles.

That’s roughly as much power as you can get from a typical highway fast-charging station, without ever having to stop to use it.

But this technology isn’t unique. Engineers around the world have already demonstrated that charging vehicles while they drive is possible.

And some of the most impressive work is happening right here in America.

Earlier this year, researchers at Purdue University revealed they’d successfully charged an electric semi-truck while it was traveling down a public highway at 65 miles per hour.

Working with the Indiana Department of Transportation and commercial vehicle manufacturer Cummins (CMI), the researchers installed wireless charging equipment beneath a quarter-mile stretch of highway in West Lafayette, Indiana.

Image: Purdue University/Photo by Kelsey Lefever

As the specially equipped truck drove over the pavement, the system transferred electricity directly to its battery.

And we’re not talking about a mere trickle of power.

It delivered between 50 and 190 kilowatts of electricity while the truck was moving, with power-transfer efficiency approaching 85%. In other words, it received enough electricity to significantly extend its driving range, with very little energy lost in the process.

Other entities are also working on this technology.

In Detroit, Israeli technology company Electreon helped build America’s first public wireless charging roadway in 2023. The quarter-mile installation uses coils embedded beneath the pavement to charge specially equipped vehicles as they drive over it.

Meanwhile, Florida is developing a three-quarter-mile wireless charging section of State Road 516, a new highway being built near Orlando. That project is designed to deliver up to 200 kilowatts of power to compatible vehicles, roughly as much as a powerful public fast-charging station.

And overseas, a company called Electreon has already demonstrated even greater charging power on France’s A10 motorway. During testing, its system delivered more than 200 kilowatts on average to a heavy-duty truck, with peak power exceeding 300 kilowatts.

Of course, these are still small-scale tests. But they prove that the technology can work on real roads.

Even the federal government is getting involved.

The Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) is supporting research into wireless charging roads, including the project in Indiana.

But the reality is that installing charging equipment beneath existing highways is expensive. One Indiana feasibility study estimated that a wireless charging lane could cost more than $6 million per mile.

Still, there may be a practical way to introduce the technology without rebuilding the entire highway system.

And it starts with America’s trucking industry.

Electric semi-trucks need enormous batteries to haul heavy loads over long distances. These batteries are expensive, heavy and take up valuable space.

But if trucks could recharge while driving, they wouldn’t need nearly as much battery power onboard.

That could mean smaller, lighter and cheaper batteries, more room for cargo and a much more practical way to power long-distance trucking.

Commercial trucking could also make the technology more affordable to roll out.

Unlike passenger vehicles, which travel all over the place, commercial trucks often follow the same shipping routes. That means we wouldn’t need to electrify every highway.

We could simply start with the busy trucking routes where thousands of vehicles travel the same roads every day.

Here’s My Take

What excites me the most about Honda’s announcement is that it offers a potential solution to one of the biggest headaches of owning an electric vehicle.

Instead of building bigger batteries or faster charging stations, we could make charging part of the driving experience.

It’s the kind of breakthrough that could give the EV market a much-needed jolt.

data.title: Poland’s Imported Inflation Meets A Cooling Domestic Economy
data.description:
October data points to a loss of momentum in Poland’s economy, with weak industrial and construction output and a cooling labour market. Inflation remains elevated, but the energy shock has yet to generate indirect or second-round effects. The central bank is ready to hike rates if needed, but does it need to?

Warsaw, Poland

The latest batch of October data points to softer economic conditions in Poland than in previous months. Even taking negative calendar effects (one fewer working day) into consideration, annual growth in both industrial and construction output still came in well below our and market expectations. Producer prices are soaring, but consumer price growth remains driven almost entirely by higher petrol prices, while wage pressures remain contained.

Industrial output weak in October

Industrial output increased by just 0.1% year-on-year in October, remaining in positive territory only thanks to robust growth in mining (+9.3% YoY) and energy supply (+1.7% YoY). Manufacturing output fell by 0.4% YoY. Sharp declines remain visible in industries struggling with rising competition from China: wearing apparel (-15.9% YoY), textiles (-6.5% YoY), furniture (-6.5% YoY) and automotive (-6.6% YoY). Double-digit growth was recorded only in the manufacture of machinery and equipment (+18.0% YoY), and more broadly in the intermediate goods production (6.2% YoY), capital goods by (1.3% YoY), and non-durable consumer goods by (1.2% YoY).

Price growth in manufacturing accelerated to 8.3% YoY in October, but wage growth in this sector eased to 4.9% YoY, the slowest pace since February 2021. With pressure from rising energy prices mounting and Chinese competition at play, businesses are reluctant to raise wages. At the same time, wage demands remain contained as employment in manufacturing continues to decline.

Construction remains in contraction

Following a sharp decline in September (-9.0% YoY), construction output fell even more sharply in October (-9.3% YoY), as the boost from public investment, driven in part by the Domestic Recovery and Resilience Programme, is fading. By early October, the authorities had sent nearly 80% of Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) grants to final beneficiaries.

Building construction remains weak as the housing market continues to suffer from oversupply, while civil engineering is losing momentum. We are still trying to determine whether the double-digit increase in construction output ahead of the August RRF grant deadline cannibalised activity in the months that followed. However, with a significant pipeline of RRF transfers (mainly in the form of loans) yet to be disbursed, the construction sector should continue to receive support in the months ahead.

Labour market not generating price pressures

The average wage in the enterprise sector rose by 6.1% YoY in October and has stabilised at around 6.0% YoY in recent months. Higher fuel prices, and consequently higher CPI inflation, have translated into slower real wage growth in recent months. There are no signs that employees are demanding higher wages to compensate for faster price growth.

Downward pressure on real disposable income, together with an elevated propensity to save, is translating into slower consumption growth. This should reduce price pressures in the economy, or at least keep them concentrated in areas directly affected by the current energy shock. Weak demand may also discourage businesses from raising the prices of their products.

Rate hikes uncertain as the economy slows

Since the outbreak of conflict in the Middle East, the market has continued to price in substantial monetary tightening in Poland (currently 75bp), but the picture is more complicated than elevated headline inflation alone would suggest. Headline inflation is high, the prolonged energy crisis increases the risk of broader price increases, other central banks are raising rates, and the zloty is weaker. At the same time, the labour market is cooling, wage pressures remain contained, there are no signs of indirect or second-round effects in price developments, and the domestic economy is clearly slowing.

A potential rate hike in the first quarter of 2027 could aim to prevent a de-anchoring of inflation expectations, although this may not represent a material risk given broader economic conditions. So far, the rise in inflation has been imported rather than driven by domestic factors.

The central bank’s macroeconomic projection points to high inflation in the first half of 2027, prompting more hawkish commentary from some Monetary Policy Council members – although the National Bank of Poland has softened its tone recently. We still expect monetary tightening in 1Q27, but the central bank could postpone the move until March or even deliver less than the 50bp of rate hikes we had previously expected. We still believe further rate hikes remain possible, as a longer-lasting or larger-than-expected energy shock may trigger broader-based price increases and eventually require a response from the NBP in the form of some monetary policy tightening.

data.title: Stock Market Correction 2026: Is It 2018 All Over Again?
data.description:
Wall Street calls the 2026 stock market correction a replay of 2018, but the differences matter more for what investors do next.

Key Takeaways

  • Stocks have done roughly half the work of the 2018 stock market selloff. Credit, the front end of the yield curve, and the “safe havens” haven’t followed the script.

  • The economy and earnings look nothing like they did in late 2018. Third-quarter GDP grew 3.4% and third-quarter earnings rose 31.9%.

  • The Fed is the difference that hurts. Powell backed off within 16 days in 2018. Today, futures price in roughly 75 basis points of additional tightening.

  • Systematic positioning is washed out, and year-end rebalancing is likely to favor buying stocks. Hedge funds protecting their annual numbers may stay defensive until January.

  • Our read is that this is a correction inside a bull market until credit or Treasuries say otherwise. The December 16 close is the line in the sand.

On Christmas Eve 2018, a client called Goldman Sachs’ derivatives desk to ask why stocks were down so much. Brian Garrett’s answer was honest: “absolutely zero idea.” Eight years later, Garrett is fielding the same calls, and nearly every desk has reached for the same playbook. The 2018 selloff is now the favorite comparison for the 2026 stock market correction.

The resemblance is real. The S&P 500 closed Friday at 6,910, down 11.6% from its October 6 record of 7,818.93 and 6% below its 200-day moving average.3 The Fed is hiking. Dealers are short gamma. The VIX closed at 37.24, above its level on Christmas Eve 2018. Garrett’s math says that if the 2018 path plays out from here, the S&P bottoms near 6,294 in the first week of January.1

However, the problem with analogies is that they rarely repeat the same way twice. As such, analogies are only useful if you check where they break. Lay 2026 next to 2018 and the price action matches, but almost nothing that produced the 2018 low has shown up yet. That gap is where both the opportunity and the risk live, and it’s what this piece is about.

Where The 2026 Stock Market Correction Looks Like 2018

Start with what matches. In late 2018, the market faced a Fed hiking into weakness, a broken 200-day moving average and a wave of systematic selling into thin holiday trading. Every one of those boxes is checked today. Garrett summed up the 2018 ingredients in his note to clients on Friday. To wit:

“A hawkish fed, technical breakdowns, extreme volatility, systematic supply, etc… sound familiar?” – Brian Garrett, Goldman Sachs, Weekend Prep, Nov. 20, 2026

Garrett measured every major asset’s move since the October 6 peak against its move between September 24 and December 24, 2018. Through Thursday, the Nasdaq 100 had completed 69% of its 2018 drawdown. The S&P 500 had done 42% and the Russell 2000 just 24%.1 Friday’s slide pushed those numbers higher, and the damage is concentrated exactly where 2018’s was: in the leaders.

The internals tell the same story. Thursday’s advance-decline spread of -426 was the worst reading of the year. One-month implied volatility for the average S&P stock is in the 93rd percentile over the past decade.2 Nvidia, the poster child of the “AI trade,” is down roughly 39% from early October. That’s what a liquidation looks like.

The first-half winners are paying for it. Across 2,258 Goldman baskets, the better a theme performed in the first half of the year, the worse it has done since, with baskets that more than doubled through June now showing a median second-half return of about -50% while the bottom four deciles have barely moved at all.1 Such is how a crowded trade unwinds.

What Makes The 2026 Stock Market Correction Different?

Here’s where the analogy starts to fall apart, and it does so in ways that cut both ways. Some differences argue that the “2018 replay” crowd is too bearish. One argues they may not be bearish enough.

The Economy Is Not Rolling Over

By the fourth quarter of 2018, growth had peaked. Real GDP slowed from a 3.4% annualized pace in the third quarter to 2.2% in the fourth.13 The tax-cut boost was fading, housing had stalled and the trade war was weighing on manufacturing and global trade. Markets were discounting the slowdown that showed up in 2019. Today, the data says something else entirely. Real GDP also grew at a 3.4% annualized rate in the third quarter, but there’s no fade. The Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow model tracked fourth-quarter growth at the same 3.4% pace as of November 17.5

Recessions don’t start with the economy growing faster than 3%. Growth can certainly slow from here. But a strong economy isn’t the setup that produces an earnings-driven bear market. The labor market’s “low hire, low fire” pattern still reads to me as labor hoarding, not the front edge of layoffs.

Earnings Are Rising, Not Getting Cut

In late 2018, tariffs, a strong dollar and slowing Chinese growth ate into corporate guidance. Analysts cut fourth-quarter estimates 3.8% during the quarter and cut first-half 2019 estimates 4.5% between mid-October and mid-January. Negative fourth-quarter guidance outnumbered positive guidance by 72 to 33.14 This time, third-quarter earnings grew 31.9%.3 Analysts raised fourth-quarter estimates 1.4% in October, and positive guidance outnumbered negative guidance by 43 to 32.15

When prices fall while forward earnings rise, valuations compress, and that’s a very different animal than an earnings recession.

The caveat is that much of that growth is driven by the AI buildout. The market is repricing what it’s willing to pay for those earnings, which makes this a valuation and liquidity event. Valuation events can still hurt, of course. They just don’t usually require a recession to end.

Iran Is An Oil Shock. The Trade War Was A Growth Shock.

The 2018 trade war directly hit corporate margins and global growth. In September 2018, Washington imposed 10% tariffs on $200 billion of Chinese imports, with a scheduled increase to 25% on January 1, and that uncertainty froze capital spending. The Iran conflict works through a different channel. Since the war began at the end of February, disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz have kept crude prices elevated.12 That’s why oil has fallen only about 7% since the October peak, compared with a 41% collapse in late 2018.1

That economic shock is now fading for consumers as gasoline futures have fallen roughly 45% between September 24 and mid-November, and the national average at the pump dropped about 13% in a month.4 Retail prices lag wholesale by weeks, so more relief is coming. This is the “bad inflation” I’ve argued cures itself. A supply shock raises prices without raising incomes, so demand eventually breaks the price. Falling gasoline works like a tax cut that lands in the first quarter, right when the 2018 analogy says the economy should be struggling.

The Fed Is The Difference That Hurts

This is the part the bulls don’t want to hear. In 2018, Jerome Powell hiked on December 19, watched stocks crater into Christmas, and turned “patient” on January 4. The “Fed put” sat close to the market because inflation was running near 2%, which gave the Fed room to back off quickly.

Today, the Fed is hiking INTO a selloff with inflation running hot. The October minutes showed almost all participants saw further increases as likely appropriate. Two even suggested a move larger than 25 basis points. Fed funds futures price roughly 75 basis points of additional tightening.4 The rates market agrees. Ten-year swaps have done 64% of their 2018 rally, but 2-year swaps have moved just 2 basis points, or 7% of the 2018 move.1 The front end of the curve isn’t pricing a rescue.

The Fed put still exists. But with inflation running hot, its strike sits much further below the market than it did in 2018, which means the Fed probably needs to see more damage in stocks, credit, or employment before it blinks, and that damage is precisely the ingredient that turned a correction into a 20% decline eight years ago. That’s the risk to plan around.

Credit Hasn’t Confirmed, And The Hedges Failed

Garrett calls credit spreads the single largest difference between now and 2018. Investment-grade CDX is just 5 basis points wider than at its peak, or 15% of its 2018 move. High yield is 38 basis points wider, which is 28% of the 136 basis points it widened in 2018. A full replay would require roughly 98 more basis points of high-yield widening.1 As I’ve written before, credit spreads are the market’s early warning system, and so far that system is mostly quiet.

Meanwhile, the “safe havens” have gone the wrong way. Gold rose 5% during the 2018 decline. This time it’s down 10.8%, and the yen is weaker against the dollar.1 A hedge that falls alongside the asset it’s hedging is just another long position. Treasuries have done their job, rallying as stocks fell, which is the behavior you’d expect in a growth scare rather than a funding crisis.

So, let’s consolidate all these points into a single table. There are certainly things we must watch as investors over the next few weeks, particularly the Fed and the credit markets. However, when gold and the yen get sold right alongside stocks, that’s the signature of a “liquidation” event, where investors sell what they can rather than what they want. Combined with rising earnings estimates, steady economic growth, and credit spreads that have barely moved, the evidence points to a de-risking sell-off more than a fundamental shift.

Who Is Left To Sell In The 2026 Stock Market Correction?

Positioning suggests the 2026 stock market correction may be friendlier than in 2018, at least in the near term. Every year, the same question arises: who still has to sell, and who has to buy? Right now the answers point in different directions depending on the cohort.

Start with the machines. Trend-following CTAs were already deeply short before last week’s leg lower. Citadel Securities put their positioning at -3.3 standard deviations as of November 4.7 When systematic funds are already short, most of their forced selling is behind them. They become buyers once volatility calms and trends stabilize. Such is the asymmetry that rarely gets discussed at the bottom of a flush.

Fundamental hedge funds have also cut risk hard. Goldman’s prime brokerage book saw net leverage fall 4.2 points to 73.4% in October.8 Morgan Stanley data shows long/short gross exposure down 10.7% since late June, with U.S. net leverage dropping five points in a single session to 42%.9 The concern is the multi-strategy platforms. PivotalPath estimates the ten largest run about $2.2 trillion in gross assets. The pod-based platforms are levered 8 to 14 times net capital and hold increasingly similar positions.10 That overlap is where a forced-selling accident could still come from.

December adds a behavioral wrinkle. For many funds, performance fees are calculated on the December 31 marks. A manager sitting on a decent year after a brutal second half has every reason to protect it rather than add risk into a falling tape. That argues for hedge fund buying power showing up in January rather than December.

Then there’s the rebalancing math. Pensions, target-date funds and balanced mandates rebalance back to fixed weights at quarter-end and year-end. With the S&P below where it began the quarter and Treasuries rallying, those portfolios are drifting underweight stocks. The mechanical year-end rebalance points toward buying equities and selling bonds, the opposite of the flow investors usually face after a strong year. Retail has also been a steady bid, with Citadel reporting 22 straight sessions of net retail buying through early November.7

A question landing in my inbox this weekend: “If everyone is already sold out, doesn’t that make this the bottom?” Not necessarily. Light positioning indicates that forced sellers are running out of ammunition. It doesn’t tell you what happens if credit cracks or the Fed hikes 50 basis points on December 9. In 2018, sentiment was already deeply bearish by mid-December, and the S&P still fell nearly 10% over the six sessions leading up to Christmas Eve.

December Seasonality And The 2026 Stock Market Correction

As we discussed in Friday’s commentary, the “Santa Claus rally” is real, but most investors get the timing wrong. Goldman’s data suggest that roughly 80% of the average year-end gain occurs after December 14. Since 2010, the December 5 to 14 window has averaged a 0.27% loss and finished higher in only 7 of 16 years. In 2011, 2014, 2015, and 2018, that window ranged from 3% to 3.6%. In years when the VIX started mid-November at 18 or higher, the median drawdown in the window was 3%, but the average year-end gain was still 1.34%.4

The end-of-year calendar explains why. First, the Fed meets for the last time this year on December 8th and 9th. Secondly, the corporate buyback window is expected to close around December 13th, followed by quarterly options expiration on December 18th. Lastly, mutual fund capital-gains record dates and tax-loss selling cluster in the same stretch, and this year there are plenty of AI losses to harvest. Early December has tended to be a sell-the-rally period, while mid-December weakness has been the opportunity.

This week will cram five trading days into three as the Thanksgiving holiday approaches. Thanksgiving weeks are always the wildcard. With three full sessions plus a Friday half-day, liquidity thins out, and in a market where dealers are short gamma and the options market implies a 3% move through next Friday. A thin tape can produce a rally that looks like a bottom and a drop that looks like a crash inside the same week. Don’t trust either one.

Is The 2026 Stock Market Correction A Warning Of Something Bigger?

Okay, let’s get to the one question that matters. Corrections are the price of admission for owning stocks. The danger is when the correction is the market’s early warning of a structural change. So I’m watching two things: the technical clock, and four channels that could turn this into something worse.

The clock is the 200-day moving average. In our analysis of 34 first breaks since 1950, 18 were back above the average four weeks later and averaged a 4.4% gain over the following month. The other 16 averaged a 3.5% decline. The uncomfortable part is that all eight breaks that fell 2.9% or more below the average within four sessions were still below it at week four. This one hit 6% in four sessions.3

  • Liquidity: Stressed, But Functioning: Currently, there is no question that market liquidity is impaired. The VIX curve is the most inverted since April 2025, and dealers are short gamma. The S&P has twice realized an entire week’s implied move in a single session.2 That’s equity plumbing under strain. What turns a positioning flush into a crisis is when the stress migrates into credit and funding markets. We aren’t seeing that yet.

  • Recession: Not In The Data : Growth above 3%, earnings growth above 30% and falling gasoline prices are not the ingredients of a recession over the next two quarters. Could that change? Of course. But a recession call today requires forecasting a shock rather than reading the data.

  • Credit: The One To Watch: Headline spreads are calm, but the bottom of the ladder isn’t. As Michael Lebowitz showed in his recent look at credit spreads, CCC spreads near 1,307 basis points have widened more than 500 basis points since early September. Meanwhile, BB spreads remain near the bottom of their 20-year range.11 The October Fed minutes also flagged AI-related debt growing through “complex and opaque financing structures,” with concentration, off-balance-sheet leasing and circular financing as potential loss amplifiers.4 If stress spreads from CCC into B and BB debt, the 2018 map is back in play.

  • The Fed: The Active Risk: This is the channel with a date attached. A 50-basis-point hike on December 9 into a falling market with credit starting to widen is how a correction becomes something larger. The other tell is Treasuries. As long as bonds rally when stocks fall, the market is pricing a growth scare. If Treasuries sell off alongside stocks, the market is pricing a policy mistake, and that’s a far more dangerous phase.

“The 2018 analogy is right about the price and wrong about the cause. Until credit or the Fed confirms it, treat this as a correction and treat every rally as a rental.”

6,294

Where the S&P 500 lands if the full 2018 path plays out, roughly 9% below Friday's close of 6,910.

So which is it? Today, the evidence says the 2026 stock market correction is just that, a correction within an ongoing bull market. The economy is growing, earnings are rising, and credit hasn’t confirmed the equity panic. However, I’d hold that view loosely. The Fed has taken away the fast rescue that ended 2018, and the CCC market is already showing the kind of stress that spreads if nobody steps in.

Rules For Handling The 2026 Stock Market Correction

The obvious question from this analysis is “Why not just sell everything and wait for clarity?” The problem, as always, is our own behavioral flaws. Clarity always shows up after the bottom, at higher prices. Selling everything 12% off the highs locks in the damage and leaves you guessing about re-entry. Rules work better than reactions, so here are the ones we’re following.

One last thought. Bob Farrell’s Rule #9 warns that when all the experts and forecasts agree, something else will happen. Right now, every desk on Wall Street agrees that this is 2018. That consensus alone makes me skeptical of a clean replay, in either direction. The rules aren’t a timing tool. They’re a reminder to stay humble when the crowd is certain.

Bottom Line

The 2018 selloff ended when credit broke, and the Fed blinked. Until one of those happens in the 2026 stock market correction, treat every rally as a chance to rebalance.

A bounce is likely coming, probably sooner than most expect. Whether it marks the bottom depends on two markets most stock investors never look at.

Questions This Article Answers

Is the 2026 stock market correction like the 2018 selloff?

The price action is similar. The S&P 500 is down 11.6% from its October 6 record, versus a 19.8% decline in late 2018. However, credit spreads, short-term rates and safe havens have not followed the 2018 pattern, and the economy and earnings are far stronger than they were in late 2018.

What was the biggest difference between 2018 and today?

The Federal Reserve. In 2018, the Fed signaled patience within 16 days of its December hike. In 2026, the Fed is hiking into hot inflation, and futures price roughly 75 basis points of further tightening, so investors shouldn’t count on a quick rescue.

Will year-end rebalancing help the stock market?

Probably at the margin. Pensions and balanced funds that rebalance to fixed weights are likely underweight stocks after the decline, which favors equity buying into December 31. CTAs are already short, which limits further systematic selling. Hedge funds protecting annual returns may wait until January to add risk.

What would signal that the 2026 stock market correction is turning into something bigger?

Watch three things: high-yield spreads widening by roughly another 100 basis points, the S&P 500 still below its 200-day average at the December 16 close, and Treasuries selling off alongside stocks rather than rallying.

data.title: Major Equity Indices Suffer Technical Damage Last Week
data.description:
With some FOMC members toying with the idea of a half-point increase in next month’s meeting, October’s PCE due out Wednesday is being watched keenly. This includes equity bulls who were humbled last week.

On Wednesday, October’s PCE (personal consumption expenditures) will be published, and this has the potential to sway FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee) votes.

Particularly after Kevin Warsh took over the Federal Reserve in May, inflation has once again been thrown into the spotlight. He has been doggedly maintaining that inflation remains elevated. The Fed targets two percent, but consumer inflation has exceeded that threshold for over five years now.

In October, CPI (consumer price index) came in stronger than expected, with both the headline and core rising 0.4 percent month over month, and the readings were 0.1 percentage point higher than the consensus. Hence the importance of Wednesday’s PCE, which is the Fed’s favorite.

In September, headline and core PCE grew 3.65 percent and 3.12 percent from a year ago, in that order. May’s 3.82 percent and 3.16 percent were the highest since May 2023 and February 2024 respectively (Chart 1). These are high readings and have been that way for a while.

Depending on how PCE behaves in October, there is a possibility that traders will begin to give some thought to the chances of a 50-basis-point increase next month, slated for 8-9.

In the last meeting – October 27-28 – the fed funds rate was held steady at a range of 3.75 percent to four percent; in the prior meeting in September, for the first time since July 2023, the benchmark rate was raised by a quarter point (Chart 2).

As things stand, a 25-basis-point hike is priced in for next month, followed by another of similar increment by next March. But policymakers of late have also been mulling over a 50. Governor Christopher Waller in recent weeks has opined that they should consider 50 basis points next month.

Minutes for the October meeting were released last Wednesday, and it was revealed that two members suggested a 50-basis-point hike. Two others – Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack – dissented in favor of a 25-basis-point increase in a 10-2 vote and could ask for more should PCE not behave.

Alternatively, markets could begin to price in two quarter-point hikes, instead of one, next year. Or, the 10-year treasury yield, which dropped 24 basis points last week to 4.91 percent – just above horizontal support at 4.75s-4.81s – could reassert itself; the rate has been under pressure since ticking 5.36 percent on October 5.

A repricing in the interest-rate outlook – should one occur – would have come at a time when equities already are on the back foot, and it is tough to tell if this might discourage the bulls even more.

The S&P 500 peaked at 7845 on October 6 and was down 12.3 percent through last Friday’s session low 6833, before closing at 6910, down 8.6 percent for the week. Last week’s tumble cost the bulls not one, not two but three levels of support – the 200-day moving average at 7349, horizontal at 7300 and rising trendline from the April 2025 low (Chart 3). From that low through the October peak, the large cap index was up 62.2 percent, and 24.2 percent from this March’s low. These are massive gains.

The March 2026 bottom followed downward pressure after the index tried for four months through February but failed to take out 6900-7000. The hurdle was finally taken care of in April. With last week’s decline, the index has now completed a round trip to that level, and the bulls have an opportunity to regroup here. Inability to do so would raise the odds that the S&P 500 would just continue toward 6100-6300. In this scenario, indicators such as the percent of S&P 500 stocks above their 50- and 200-day (43.2 percent and 48.8 percent respectively) have the potential to reach extreme oversold levels, laying the foundation for a sound low.

Over on the Nasdaq 100, 32 percent and 36 percent of the constituent stocks are above the 50- and 200-day; this is low given 59.4 percent and 65.4 percent were above the averages late October and early this month respectively but do not yet represent washout levels.

On the index itself, there was a sense of panic last Thursday and Friday, as the tech-heavy index collapsed 10.4 percent to 25029 for the week. On October 6, it peaked at 31361. From that high to Friday’s session low 24910, the Nasdaq 100 is down 20.6 percent, which is quite a drop in and of itself, but some perspective is in order here. From the lows of March this year and April last year, the Nasdaq 100 surged 37.3 percent and 89.6 percent respectively. Bulls, particularly those that got in early, are probably not panicking just yet.

That said, the index has been dealt some damage. The 200-day (28073) has been compromised. Ditto with trendline support from the April 2025 low, not to mention horizontal support at 26100s, which is where the bears are likely to show up should a reflex rally evolve in the sessions ahead.

In small-caps, bulls last week were unable to stop the bears from claiming 2700. For the week, the Russell 2000 dove 7.5 percent to 2582, down 16.1 percent from the August 14 peak of 3070. After that peak, the index then kept bleeding for nine weeks before finding support just north of 2700, where it went sideways for five weeks, but only to breach the level last week. A rising trendline from the low of April last year has been violated as well (Chart 5).

Not surprisingly, the index is grossly oversold, particularly on the daily. A reflex rally is always possible, but should one develop, this likely will be used as an opportunity by the bears to reload and short at 2700.

data.title: The Bank Of Israel Leaves Its Policy Rate Unchanged Despite Very Low Inflation
data.description:
Today’s decision by the Bank of Israel to stand pat results from a mixture of different forces hitting the shekel, some positive, others negative. The policy rate remains at 3.25%, a decision that will remain intact until the next meeting in early January 2027. While there is no clear winner from the October 27th election, this short window still introduces considerable uncertainty as to the nation’s immediate future.

On balance, one would expect a rate cut today, given that Israel has the lowest inflation rate in the OECD. In October the CPI fell by 0.1%, and the 12-month inflation gauge is 1.1%, even below the Bank’s midpoint target of 1% to 3%. What held the rate decision in check was the deterioration in the shekel, losing nearly 8% against the dollar and 5% against the euro. With imports costing more, the Bank expects the inflation rate to pick up during the next 6 months.

Source; Gemini

In the spring and summer of 2026, the shekel appreciation enabled rate cuts. Now, the tables are slightly turned as the shekel depreciates along with political uncertainty, all the while inflation is virtually non-existent. , 

Also holding back a rate cut is that the GDP grew at a very robust rate of 8% in the third quarter relative to the previous quarter. Private consumption, business investment, and exports all grew at very high rates. Israeli statisticians strip out the performance of Israeli firms overseas from national income calculations. GDP net of production overseas still grew at a healthy rate of 4%. The economy does not exhibit any weaknesses in key sectors that would prompt the Bank to offer more monetary stimulus.

Turning to the external sector, the current account, usually in surplus, slid into deficit in the first two quarters of the year. Countering this is a surge in Foreign Direct Investment headed for the tech. Over US$ 15 billion has been invested in Israel so far, providing the obvious explanation for the USD/ILA hitting a historic low of 2.8 earlier in the year. Lastly, the cumulative deficit from government expenditures in the past 12 months is running at 3.3 % of GDP, and remains below the government’s deficit target.  

So, the Bank was faced with a dilemma this month. Cut the rate in response to a very low inflation rate. Or hold the rate in the face of an inconclusive election result that may extend into the new year. Cutting the bank rate also risked a widening of the US-Israel interest rate spread, which would result in capital outflows and a further deterioration in the shekel. As long as other major central bankers talk up the need to raise rates to combat inflation, the Bank of Israel made the right decision to keep the spread from widening. Moreover, the strength of the domestic economy confirms that a rate cut is not necessary to promote growth.

data.title: The Nvidia Flip-Flop Sends Stocks Into Orbit, But The AI Circus Isn't Out Of The Woods
data.description:
Takeaways by The Dark Side of the Boom

• Wall Street has witnessed one of the most extraordinary corporate U-turns in recent memory, and the return of Nvidia's (NVDA) larger-than-life founder has delivered a rally that even the most battle-hardened trading desks will remember.

• Beneath the spectacular headlines, a violent unwinding of short positions and options hedges has exposed just how fragile market liquidity has become, raising questions about the staying power of the rebound.

• The bond market, dollar and commodities are telling a rather more complicated story than the jubilant equity screens suggest, with some familiar relationships being turned on their heads.

• Washington may have helped put the AI locomotive back on the tracks, but the political, regulatory and financial obstacles ahead haven’t disappeared simply because its most famous conductor has returned.

The King Is Back, and Wall Street Throws the Biggest Party Since Liberation Day

Well, you couldn’t make this stuff up. Just when Wall Street had spent the better part of a fortnight writing Nvidia’s obituary, questioning the future of the AI revolution and wondering whether the entire technology complex was about to disappear down a financial rabbit hole, Jensen Huang walked back through the front door of Nvidia headquarters and the market promptly went absolutely bananas. In one of the most extraordinary corporate reversals in recent memory, Nvidia’s board reinstated its former chief executive following direct intervention from President Trump, with Vice President Vance reportedly enlisted to help push the process along. Whatever one makes of the governance implications, the market’s verdict was delivered with all the subtlety of a wrecking ball.

Nvidia surged 31%, adding a staggering $952 billion in market value in a single session, while the Nasdaq 100 rocketed 6.9%, the S&P 500 jumped 4.7%, and the semiconductor index exploded 14%. It was Wall Street’s biggest celebration since Trump paused his Liberation Day tariffs in April 2025, and for anyone unfortunate enough to have been leaning heavily short into Monday’s opening bell, it must have felt like being run over by the AI express train just as they thought it had finally derailed.

The irony is delicious. Only days earlier, the market had been treating Nvidia like a corporate crime scene, with the company’s leadership crisis, regulatory investigations and mounting political controversy threatening to pull the rug from beneath the entire AI investment complex. Now the same stock was being chased higher with almost religious enthusiasm, as though the return of one man had magically restored the industry’s earnings forecasts, repaired its financing problems and settled every uncomfortable question about the enormous capital expenditure required to keep the AI machine humming.

Huang’s importance to Nvidia is unquestionably extraordinary. He is not merely the company’s chief executive but its principal dealmaker, industry evangelist and strategic architect, with an influence that stretches from semiconductor design to data-centre investment and the complicated relationships linking AI laboratories, hyperscalers and their suppliers. His reinstatement restores a familiar hand to the wheel, and that has genuine value for investors trying to assess the company’s strategic direction.

But there is a rather uncomfortable distinction between restoring confidence in Nvidia’s leadership and repairing the financial foundations of the entire AI boom.

Wall Street may have got its king back, but the kingdom still has a few unpaid bills.

And judging by the extraordinary violence of Monday’s price action, much of the rally had less to do with investors suddenly discovering a new earnings outlook than with traders being caught spectacularly on the wrong side of an overcrowded book.

The Mother of All Short Squeezes Meets a Market With No Liquidity

The opening explosion in Nvidia was accompanied by a wholesale demolition of bearish positioning, with leveraged short products suffering devastating losses and options traders scrambling to unwind hedges built during the previous week’s panic. The initial burst of call buying, dealer hedging and short covering produced the kind of price action that makes the trading desk feel like a casino where somebody has suddenly turned the lights back on and announced that every losing ticket is now a winner.

But the most revealing detail wasn’t how far the market jumped. It was what happened after the opening fireworks.

Nvidia held much of its extraordinary advance, yet the buying failed to accelerate meaningfully beyond the initial surge. The Nasdaq recovered sharply, but was still only returning to levels last seen around the previous Tuesday’s lows, while the major indices remained below their 200-day moving averages. For all the champagne being sprayed around Wall Street, the broader technical damage hadn’t disappeared.

And then there was liquidity, or rather the astonishing lack of it.

Top-of-book liquidity in the S&P 500 futures market was reportedly around $2.5 million, the sort of depth that would have raised eyebrows on a quiet summer afternoon, never mind during one of the largest technology rallies in years. Hedge funds were doing much of the heavy lifting, aggressively buying technology shares and ETFs, while traditional long-only investors were modest net sellers on substantially smaller volumes. Retail favourites and previously crowded winners enjoyed explosive rebounds, but the underlying flow suggested a market being driven by positioning rather than a broad institutional stampede back into equities.

There is a world of difference between a market rising because everybody wants to own it and one rising because nobody can afford to remain short.

The options market offered another clue. The VIX retreated sharply as protective positions were unwound, yet at approximately 28.9 it remained unusually elevated for a session in which the S&P 500 had surged close to 5%. More troubling was the VVIX, the volatility of volatility itself, which remained above 118 and in the 93rd percentile of its historical distribution. In plain dealing-room English, investors had stopped paying quite so much for immediate protection, but they were still paying a handsome premium for insurance against the next nasty surprise.

The extraordinary dislocation across momentum strategies reinforced the picture. Longer-term momentum dramatically outperformed shorter-term signals, with the spread between twelve-month and three- or six-month momentum reaching record territory. Correlations between these strategies were breaking down, creating precisely the sort of violent crosscurrents that can turn sophisticated quantitative portfolios into very expensive washing machines.

This wasn’t the orderly return of confidence. It was a market violently repricing the probability of disaster after discovering that one of its largest assumptions had changed overnight.

And while the shorts were being carried out on stretchers, another supposed beneficiary of the AI renaissance was conspicuously missing from the celebrations.

Anthropic fell 1.4%, despite the introduction of listed options, with the world’s largest IPO still struggling to put meaningful distance between its share price and the $83 offering level. That divergence deserves attention. Nvidia’s leadership uncertainty may have been dramatically reduced, but investors were clearly not prepared to extend the same enthusiasm to every corner of the AI ecosystem.

The financing question hasn’t gone away, and neither has the uncomfortable debate over whether frontier laboratories and neocloud operators can generate the revenues needed to meet their enormous computing commitments.

The Trump Put Arrives, but the Fed Sends the Bill

If equity traders were celebrating the return of the Trump put, the bond market was busy reminding everyone that policy interventions have consequences. Last week’s equity liquidation had driven investors into Treasuries, with two-year yields falling approximately 20 basis points as traders scaled back expectations for aggressive Fed tightening. Monday’s spectacular equity rebound reversed some of that defensive positioning, pushing short-dated yields higher as the market began pricing a greater likelihood of further rate increases.

The initial Treasury selloff was perfectly understandable. With the immediate threat to the AI investment cycle apparently diminished, some of the urgency to seek shelter in government bonds evaporated. But as the session progressed, the picture became considerably more interesting.

Oil prices began collapsing, dragging inflation expectations lower and attracting renewed demand for longer-dated Treasuries. By the close, long-end yields had fallen roughly 3–4 basis points, leaving the curve sharply flatter even as the equity market was enjoying its biggest party in eighteen months.

That is a rather curious combination. The equity market was celebrating the restoration of its favourite growth champion, the short end was acknowledging a potentially more hawkish Fed, and the long bond was finding support as crude oil tumbled and inflation concerns eased.

The dollar, meanwhile, was having none of the equity market’s newfound enthusiasm for risk. The greenback strengthened again, extending a remarkable run of gains across nine of the previous ten sessions and continuing to tighten global financial conditions even as US stocks surged.

This is one of the more important cross-asset signals from Monday’s session. A genuine improvement in global risk appetite would ordinarily provide some relief to higher-beta currencies and reduce demand for defensive dollar liquidity, yet the greenback continued marching higher. That suggests the broader financial squeeze has not simply disappeared because Nvidia has recovered some of its lost market capitalization.

Wall Street may have received a presidential rescue package, but the Fed still controls the price of money, and the dollar is making sure nobody forgets it.

Wednesday’s core PCE inflation report now becomes the next major test. A softer reading could encourage expectations that the Fed’s hawkishness is approaching its peak, potentially giving equities another leg higher. But another uncomfortable inflation print would leave investors confronting the same monetary-policy dilemma that helped fuel the original liquidation.

Oil Takes the Elevator Down While Gold Finds Its Feet

If Monday’s equity rally was all fireworks and champagne, the energy complex looked as though somebody had cancelled Christmas.

WTI crude plunged more than 3% toward $80 a barrel, while Brent slipped below $90 to its lowest level since August as investors unwound geopolitical risk premiums following indications that Washington might allow diplomacy with Iran more time. The reopening of Libya’s Sharara pipeline, restoring approximately 350,000 barrels a day of disrupted supply, added to the downward pressure, while weakness in gasoline, heating oil and refining margins reinforced the increasingly bearish petroleum picture.

Natural gas joined the rout, with US front-month futures tumbling as much as 9.1% intraday before settling roughly 6% lower near $3.50. Warmer weather forecasts across the Midwest and eastern US had traders rapidly dismantling winter-demand expectations. Europe initially moved in the opposite direction, with colder forecasts pushing TTF gas sharply higher before that rally also evaporated by the close.

For the broader market, cheaper energy is potentially useful medicine. Lower fuel costs can relieve pressure on household budgets, reduce corporate expenses and do some of the Fed’s inflation-fighting work without another turn of the monetary-policy screw. But there is always a catch: falling oil prices are considerably less comforting when they reflect weakening demand rather than improving supply.

Gold managed to retain some of its early gains as demand for dollar liquidity eased, although the broader metals complex faded from its initial highs. Bitcoin (BTC.X) offered an even more revealing performance, leaping on the Nvidia headlines before surrendering the entire advance as the dollar strengthened. The supposed alternative to fiat money had briefly remembered its high-beta technology credentials before discovering that a rising dollar was still an uncomfortable opponent.

The message from commodities was considerably less euphoric than the one flashing across equity screens.

The $952 Billion Question: Relief Rally or Something More Durable?

For all the extraordinary gains, Nvidia remains approximately 31% below its October 6 peak, with nearly $1.8 trillion in market value still missing from its record valuation. Monday’s rebound was spectacular, but it did not restore the previous high-water mark, repair every broken technical level or resolve the governance and regulatory questions that triggered the original crisis.

The political complications may yet prove particularly uncomfortable. Huang is scheduled to appear before congressional investigators in early December, with lawmakers from both parties pressing for tougher chip export controls and greater scrutiny of the circumstances surrounding his reinstatement. The intervention that helped restore market confidence has also intensified questions about the relationship between Washington, Nvidia and national-security policy.

For traders, the more immediate roadmap is technical.

The S&P 500’s explosive recovery has already reclaimed the initial 7,200–7,250 area, making that zone the first important test on any pullback. Sustained strength above 7,250, accompanied by improving breadth and declining volatility, would open the possibility of a move toward 7,350–7,400, with 7,450–7,500 a more ambitious extension if the short-covering and options-driven momentum continues through Thanksgiving week.

But a failure to defend 7,200 would quickly take some of the shine off Monday’s spectacular reversal, particularly if volatility begins rising again and semiconductor leadership falters. Below 7,100, attention would shift toward 7,000 and potentially Friday’s panic low near 6,883.

The distinction matters because the circumstances surrounding last Friday’s options expiration created fertile ground for a violent rebound even without a lasting improvement in the underlying fundamentals. Deeply negative dealer gamma, stretched bearish positioning and elevated volatility can produce extraordinary upside moves once selling pressure begins to ease. Monday’s rally was a textbook example of how rapidly those forces can reverse, but a genuine bottom requires the market to demonstrate that fresh buying can absorb supply after the initial short squeeze has run its course.

There is plenty to celebrate in Huang’s return. Nvidia has regained the executive who helped build one of the most consequential businesses in modern technology, and the immediate uncertainty surrounding its leadership has been dramatically reduced. Yet the company remains exposed to investigations, political scrutiny and the broader question of whether the AI investment boom can sustain its enormous financing requirements.

The more troubling issue is what Monday revealed about the market itself. A single corporate decision, apparently accelerated by intervention from the White House, was sufficient to add nearly a trillion dollars to one company’s value and ignite the largest US equity rally since April 2025, even as liquidity remained painfully thin and institutional investors showed relatively little appetite for chasing the opening surge.

Wall Street got Jensen Huang back, the shorts got taken to the woodshed, and the AI circus suddenly discovered its ringmaster was alive and well. But when nearly a trillion dollars can appear on the screen in a single session while the underlying financial plumbing remains this fragile, I’d be careful about confusing a spectacular rescue act with a market that has genuinely found its feet.

The king has returned. Whether the kingdom can afford another coronation is an entirely different question.
